title: I Was Disappointed by Miele’s Last Vacuums, but the New IFA Lineup Changed My Mind
snippet: The previous model fell short in our lab tests, so I went into my hands-on trial skeptical. I left impressed.
fullText:
With this in mind, when Miele showed me its new HX3 and HX3 Plus Aqua, I was skeptical it would be more than an incremental jump, but after spending some time using it at the Miele Experience Center in Manhattan prior to the IFA 2026 show in Berlin, I came away impressed by several of the changes. 

Miele is known as one of the most reputable brands for home appliances and cleaning, but when we lab tested the Miele HX2 cordless vacuum last year, we were a little let down by it — it performed poorly in sand tests for low and midpile carpet, and the design was a little finicky to use compared to lightweight competition from Dyson and Shark. It also cost $1,100 at full price, making it a hard sell. 

To start with, while there hasn’t been a complete redesign, one of the big changes is rebalancing the weight distribution so that more of it is at the bottom, reducing the strain up top when you’re vacuuming. You can also change out where the motor and waste bin are, depending on how you attach the nozzles, so it’s up to you how you want the weight to fall.

A Miele representative showed me an example of how you might want it more top-heavy when you’re using it to clean the corners of ceilings and higher-up spots. You can also convert it fairly easily back into the self-standing vacuum mode, a traditional stick vac or a handheld. 

There are also other quality-of-life tweaks, like push-button controls, easier dustbin emptying, finer particle capture, automatic flooring-type detection and the ability to stand upright. It offers 70 minutes of running time, which Miele says should be good enough to clean 1,700 square feet in a single charge, and some models have an extended battery included for even more juice. All key things that I value when vacuuming.  

Miele

The big improvements come in performance. The HX3 has notably better pickup on both carpet and hard flooring. The Miele representatives even helpfully provided me with some condiments to imitate sand and pet hair to try to suction up from the carpet. While it wasn’t quite the same as CNET’s rigorous lab testing, the outcome of my vacuuming session offered solid results. The HX3 was able to remove most or all of the pet hair with a single back-and-forth motion, while the imitation sand was no challenge at all on hardwood (though that’s true of most vacuums and robot vacuums we test). 

Overall, the HX3 seemed to do a great job of picking up dirt and debris from different floor types. There’s also a powerful Boost mode that can give you extra suction beyond even the highest setting, but it drains the battery the fastest, so it’s limited to just 10 seconds. 

The HX3 Plus Aqua is basically the same as the regular HX3; it just comes with Miele’s first mopping attachment, the Aqua Twister Floorhead. It consists of dual spinning mop pads that are machine washable, a 300-milliliter water tank and a 360-degree light. I also took the mopping attachment for a spin, trying out its different modes on hard flooring to clean stains and dirt. Again, the results were impressive, with the amount of water being dispensed fully adjustable, allowing you to tackle bigger messes and spills. When the mopping head is attached, Boost mode also dispenses more water for 30 seconds, so it’s good to see the feature has been integrated into both cleaning heads. 

Miele

While there are two distinct models, the HX3 and HX3 Plus Aqua, there’s a somewhat more consumer-friendly price spread: The base HX3 starts at $849, while the top-tier HX3 Aqua Plus, with all the accessories, including the mopping head, runs $1,249. There are a number of models in between, each with its own price and array of attachments, so I’m just going to lay them out in a list below, pulled from the specs sheet. 

Triflex HX3 ($849)

Included: MultiFloor XXL (SEB430), Accessory Set (dusting brush, upholstery tool, crevice nozzle, mounting clip), 1 Lithium-Ion Battery by Varta, Wall Mount with accessory storage

Triflex HX3 Hardfloor (Amazon exclusive) ($949)

Included: MultiFloor XXL (SEB430), Accessory Set (dusting brush, upholstery tool, crevice nozzle, mounting clip), Hardfloor Roller (HX-HC10), 1 Lithium-Ion Battery by Varta, Wall Mount with accessory storage

Triflex HX3 Cat & Dog ($999)

Included: MultiFloor XXL with headlight (SEB430), Accessory Set (dusting brush, upholstery tool, crevice nozzle, mounting clip), Electro Compact (HX-EC10), 1 Lithium-Ion Battery by Varta, Wall Mount with accessory storage

title: iOS 27 beta 8 now available as Apple tests major Siri AI upgrade
snippet: Apple has released the eighth iOS 27 beta for developer testing. iOS 27 beta 8 continues Apple’s summer beta cycle ahead of a public release in September. We’ll update our devices and share what we discover. Update 5:04 p.m. ET: Now available for public beta testers as well. more…
fullText:
Apple has released the eighth iOS 27 beta for developer testing. iOS 27 beta 8 continues Apple’s summer beta cycle ahead of a public release in September. We’ll update our devices and share what we discover.

Update 5:04 p.m. ET: Now available for public beta testers as well. 

Apple releases eighth iOS 27 developer beta for testing

The eighth developer beta is available now through the Settings app on eligible iPhones. If you’re enrolled in the Apple Developer Program, go to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates and choose the iOS 27 Developer Beta.

Today’s developer beta release will likely become iOS 27 public beta 6. The final version for everyone will arrive in the next few weeks.

iOS 27 is all about Siri AI

iOS 27 is one of Apple’s most AI-focused iPhone updates yet. The headline change is Siri AI, Apple’s rebuilt assistant powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence and new Apple Foundation Models.

Siri AI brings richer conversations, personal context, broader world knowledge, on-screen awareness, and deeper app actions across the system.

On iPhone, Siri AI also gets a new visual experience tied to the Dynamic Island, plus a dedicated Siri app for revisiting conversations across devices.

Visual Intelligence joins Siri too, including a new Siri mode in the Camera app and improvements that affect Camera Control on iPhone.

Apple Intelligence is also expanding across apps. iOS 27 adds AI-powered improvements for Photos, Safari, Passwords, Mail, Messages, Phone, Shortcuts, Home, and more. As we covered in our breakdown of Apple’s new Foundation Models, some capabilities run on-device, while others use Private Cloud Compute.

More iOS 27 features and changes

Beyond Siri and Apple Intelligence, iOS 27 includes a variety of iPhone-specific changes. Apple has refined the Liquid Glass design introduced last year, including a new Liquid Glass transparency slider for adjusting the look of system UI.

There are also performance improvements for app launches, Photos loading, Camera launch in Low Power Mode, AirDrop transfers, and Wi-Fi-to-cellular transitions.

Other iPhone changes include Photos keywords and star ratings, customizable slideshows, smoother Camera behavior, continuous sending in Messages, Dual Capture in FaceTime, custom EQ for AirPods, new recovery options, easier Apple Pay card switching, and AI-generated wallpaper creation.

We’re installing iOS 27 beta 8 now and will update with any notable changes. In the meantime, you can catch up on everything new in iOS 27 from Apple’s keynote list.

title: At G20, Big Tech and Global Leaders Can’t Escape AI’s Data Center Problem
snippet: Growing nationwide opposition to AI and data centers came right up to the summit’s doorstep.
fullText:
At the G20 Innovation Ministerial summit on Wednesday, US Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, on stage with Anthropic Chief Compute Officer Tom Brown, made a controversial argument: If the world wants to grow AI, we need data centers.

On the surface, this is logical. Data centers are a crucial piece of infrastructure that tech companies need to power their training of new AI models. But the first part of that “if-then” statement is questionable. These massive AI server farms are wildly unpopular, in large part because of serious environmental concerns, energy costs and resource guzzling.

Over the past few years, data center construction projects have been sprouting across the US, with about 3,400 sites already operational and another 2,000 planned, according to Cleanview’s data center tracker tool. The facilities are notorious for demanding massive amounts of electricity to power AI compute, clean water to cool the computer chips and acreage to build on.

	

			

Tech companies are quick to claim that data centers create jobs and give back to the tax base. But local residents are footing the bill and have pushed back, saying they bring noise and air pollution and higher utility bills. And the growing opposition is bipartisan: Both Democrats and Republicans (as well as independents) are against new data centers in their area. 

That’s why the US government is launching a campaign to persuade other global leaders to promote AI data centers. Will it work? 

Rising anti-Big Tech protests

The backlash against AI and Big Tech came right to the G20’s doorstep on Wednesday, as the summit is being held at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. About 100 students and local residents participated in a protest against the in-person and virtual appearances by Lutnick, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk.

UNC-Chapel Hill students and local residents gathered outside The Carolina Inn, where the G20 forum is being held.Katelyn Chedraoui/Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

“We as students and community members are showing up because we do not think that tech billionaires should feel comfortable and have a place on our campus,” said Amy, a student and member of UNC’s Sunrise organization, which advocates for social and economic justice. 

Amy, who did not provide her last name, told me that students have been protesting the addition of over 20 Flock surveillance cameras across campus. Protestors chanted, “Hey ho, hey ho, Sam Altman has got to go.” Some signs called out Lutnick’s ties to Jeffrey Epstein, while others advocated for tech companies to put people over profits.

Government response: No more doomerism

Pro-AI tactics often use a common message: Anyone who doesn’t get on board will be left behind. President Donald Trump doubled down on this claim with a post on Truth Social this week, saying that communities that don’t allow data centers to move in will end up “backwards and poor.” Beyond the inflammatory rhetoric, there’s no proof this is true.

The administration’s approach during this week’s summit has been to focus on growth, unburdened by new regulation. Lutnick and other officials are adamant that existing laws and statutes are sufficient to address any issues posed by AI and that additional rules would be burdensome. But we’ve already seen how AI can perpetrate harm under current US laws.

“This is an opportunity to democratize intelligence,” Lutnick said on Wednesday, adding that he “doesn’t buy the AI doomerism at all.” AI doomers tend to believe AI poses a serious, existential risk to humanity. 

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman (left) and US Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick on stage at the G20 forum.Katelyn Chedraoui/CNET

In an effort to assuage concerns that data centers raise people’s electric bills, the Trump administration got the biggest tech companies to sign a ratepayer protection pledge, which says tech companies, not individuals, will absorb any rising energy costs. But as CNET reported, the pledge is voluntary, and there’s no way to enforce it.

Energy constraints on the US’s already overtaxed electrical grid, combined with community opposition to data centers, could create a new incentive for tech companies to optimize their operating systems and software to run on less energy. And tech companies say that once they have sufficient energy, the excess will be returned to communities. But that’s speaking optimistically. 

Tech response: Focus on curing cancer

There’s no one better suited (or less objective) to speak about data centers than Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

“Every single country that we’ve worked with, the moment we created [AI] infrastructure locally, all of a sudden, the startups and researchers just really get activated,” Huang told G20 ministers on Wednesday. 

Huang said the US’s regulatory environment allows for substantial build-out of AI infrastructure. Though tech companies often boast that data centers create jobs, many studies say that job growth is overstated. After construction is complete, employment opportunities tend to be minimal once the site is built and running. 

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (left) on stage with Lutnick discussing AI at the G20 Innovation Ministerial.Katelyn Chedraoui/CNET

In an effort to combat data centers’ growing reputation problem, tech companies have pivoted their focus to the potential scientific advances AI could help cultivate in the future. The marketing pitch goes: If AI cures cancer, isn’t the cost worth it?

“The economic scientific impacts [of AI] that we’ll see five years from now will be immense. I think that we will make a major impact in things like curing cancer,” Anthropic’s Brown said on Wednesday. 

But Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei seems to discern that AI hype isn’t entirely effective. In August, he said that tech companies need to win back people’s trust, writing on X: “At this point, saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliché than it is inspiring, and most people think it is deceptive. The thing that will work is *actually curing cancer*.” 

That at least appears to read the room, even if it doesn’t prevent the harm data centers cause to communities in the meantime.

Local AI development gets faster

Parallels Desktop 27 also adds support for Scalable Matrix Extension (SME2) instructions in Linux and Windows VMs on M4 and newer Macs. title: AI will be the defining test of Apple’s environmental commitments, says Greenpeace
snippet: Greenpeace says the adoption of AI poses the biggest threat to Apple’s environmental track record, and argues that how the company responds will be the “defining test” of whether it really means what it says. Apple’s environmental achievements to date have been unrivalled, but the massive data center demands created by Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features could change all of that … more…
fullText:
Greenpeace says the adoption of AI poses the biggest threat to Apple’s environmental track record, and argues that how the company responds will be the “defining test” of whether it really means what it says.

Apple’s environmental achievements to date have been unrivalled, but the massive data center demands created by Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features could change all of that … 

Greenpeace has praised Apple’s environmental initiatives for more than a decade now. That included a 2015 report on the company’s use of renewable energy to power data centers.

Apple continues to lead the charge in powering its corner of the internet with renewable energy even as it continues to rapidly expand. All three of its data center expansions announced in the past year will be powered with renewable energy. Apple is also having a positive impact on pushing major colocation providers to help it maintain progress toward its 100% renewable energy goal.

Just last year, Greenpeace East Asia gave the company a B+ grade for introducing more renewable energy in its supply chains.

However, as Apple finally launches Siri AI next month, that could all change. While the company aims to carry out as many tasks as possible on-device, it relies on large-scale data centres to perform more complex actions, and these consume a great deal of electricity and water. The Verge cites concerns expressed by Greenpeace spokesperson Avex Li.

“AI will be the defining test of Apple’s climate commitments,” Li says. “To preserve Tim Cook’s environmental legacy, the company will need to show that AI growth can be accommodated within its existing climate commitments through absolute emissions reductions, additional renewable energy investment, and longer-lasting products.”

Apple responded by pointing The Verge to its most recent environmental progress report, as well as past statements on the topic.

title: TCL’s new Nxtpaper phone offers both e-reader and OLED
snippet: The “sculpted” design is more premium than other Nxtpaper phones so far. | Image: TCL With the P80 Ultra, TCL's E Ink-esque Nxtpaper phones are finally going OLED. Just like previous LCD models, the phone can switch to a low power, monochromatic display mode that replicates the look of paper when you want to read or minimize distractions. TCL first revealed the OLED Nxtpaper technology at MWC in March this year, but without any products that took advantage of it. The P80 Ultra is the first, with a 6.83-inch panel that delivers high-end OLED specs in most respects: a 1.5K resolution, 120Hz refresh rates, 3,200 nits … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
With the P80 Ultra, TCL’s E Ink-esque Nxtpaper phones are finally going OLED. Just like previous LCD models, the phone can switch to a low power, monochromatic display mode that replicates the look of paper when you want to read or minimize distractions. Only now you can switch back to what the company calls a “flagship-level” OLED experience the rest of the time.

TCL first revealed the OLED Nxtpaper technology at MWC in March this year, but without any products that took advantage of it. The P80 Ultra is the first, with a 6.83-inch panel that delivers high-end OLED specs in most respects: a 1.5K resolution, 120Hz refresh rates, 3,200 nits of peak brightness, and coverage of 100 percent of the DCI-P3 color space. In fact, TCL argues that its Nxtpaper innovations actually make this OLED better than some other flagship phones, because it benefits from an anti-glare coating that should be among the best on the market. I’ll be getting the chance to try the P80 Ultra in person at IFA this week, and I’m excited to see whether the OLED panel lives up to that promise.

Like other Nxtpaper handsets, the P80 Ultra will run just like a regular Android phone 90 percent of the time. Flick the dedicated Nxtpaper Key and it switches to Max Ink Mode though, turning the phone into something more akin to an e-reader: a monochromatic, paperlike display; a custom Android UI with fewer apps and notifications; and dedicated software to use it as an e-reader. Max Ink Mode has another benefit, extending the life of the 5,800mAh battery to a full seven days of active use, or up to 26 days of standby time.

The phone’s sculpted rear design is intended to feel fairly premium, but the remaining features fit squarely in the upper midrange market. You get 8GB of RAM and up to 512GB storage, a MediaTek Dimensity 7400 Elite chipset, and 45W wired charging. The 50-megapixel, 1/1.56-inch-type main camera should be fairly capable, though TCL’s image processing lags behind that of bigger name rivals. An 8-megapixel ultrawide doesn’t sound especially impressive, but a 50-megapixel, 3x telephoto lens is a welcome inclusion that adds versatility to the cameras.

The P80 Ultra is joined by two cheaper models. The P80 Pro features almost all the same specs, including that OLED panel, but drops to a dual rear camera, omitting the telephoto. The regular P80 is a different beast entirely: It keeps the OLED but lacks the Nxtpaper features, removing TCL’s key selling point, and runs on a smaller 5,000mAh battery.

All three phones arrive running Android 16. The Ultra and Pro will receive four years of OS updates and seven of security support, while the base P80 gets one fewer Android version update.

The new phones are launching in Europe today, with a Latin American release following in October, and the US “a bit later,” TCL told me during a press briefing. The P80 Ultra starts from €549 (about $635), the P80 Pro from €429 ($500), and the P80 from €349 ($400).

fullText:
After introducing the Thus processing chip in April and releasing it with the Liberty 5 Pro series earbuds, Soundcore is bringing it to more audio products. The Thus chip is behind the best call quality I’ve ever heard from a pair of earbuds or headphones, virtually eliminating ambient sounds from the speaker’s environment. At IFA 2026 in Berlin, Soundcore announced the Space 2 Pro headphones, AeroClip 2 and AeroClip 2 Pro open clip earbuds, and Liberty Buds 2.

The Space 2 Pro will be the first headphones to use the Thus chip and use a 6-microphone array for voice isolation. There are also eight microphones for the headphones’ adaptive active noise cancellation (ANC), which Soundcore claims is 1.5 times stronger than the ANC on the Space One Pro headphones across the 20Hz to 2,000Hz frequency range. (This covers the most important sound distractions including airplane drones and HVAC systems, as well as normal conversation.)

Soundcore’s latest version of its HearID listening preference test will create customized sound profiles, and the headphones support high-res audio via LDAC. Soundcore says the Space 2 Pro will get 60 hours of listening time at 50 percent volume (30 with ANC on) or 20 hours of talk time on a single charge. They launch on September 22 for $200, come in three colors — gray, white, and black — and will be available in the US, EU, and UK.

Soundcore is also expanding its clip earbuds offerings, updating the AeroClip and adding a Pro version. The AeroClip 2 looks to be similar to the AeroClip, but with the Thus chip, will retail for $170 (the same price as the original AeroClip), and come in black, red, white, and blue at launch on September 22.

The AeroClip 2 Pro will include Soundcore’s AI note-taking capability, which was also on the Liberty 5 Pro Max. But unlike the Liberty 5 Pro Max, with the AeroClip 2 Pro you can record online meetings and phone calls in addition to in-person interactions. The AeroClip 2 Pro includes a free AI transcription starter plan with 120 minutes per month for 24 months and the ability to subscribe for more transcription minutes. The 2 Pro clip earbuds use 11mm dual-diaphragm drivers, support LDAC hi-res audio, and should provide 10 hours of playback at 50 percent volume, with 30 hours total with the charging case. There’s no firm launch date or pricing yet for the 2 Pro, but we expect them later this year.

Finally, the Soundcore Liberty Buds 2 are small, 4.7-gram earbuds. They will also include the Thus chip for call clarity and use a 6-microphone ANC system. The Liberty Buds 2 will be available in purple, black, and white on September 22 for $130.

title: Google is making AI Overviews even bigger on some search queries
snippet: As AI continues to be a bigger and bigger part of Google Search, the company is making AI Overviews bigger on some searches. more…
fullText:
As AI continues to be a bigger and bigger part of Google Search, the company is making AI Overviews bigger on some searches.

Already placed above traditional search results, Google’s AI Overviews provide an AI-generated answer to your query, pulling that information from links around the web and placing some of those links within the answer. 

Now, those are getting bigger.

In some search queries, Google will automatically fully expand AI Overviews, effectively turning the whole page into an AI response rather than just taking up the very top of the page. The change was first spotted by Chris Long, and Google has confirmed the update to Search Engine Roundtable, saying:

	

For some queries, AI Overviews may dynamically expand for topics where our systems determine it’s most useful for people. Our research has shown that with this dynamic experience, users find Search more helpful and engage deeper in follow-up exploration.

One example of where this happens consistently is with definitions, where AI Overviews take up the entire screen.

title: Gemini 3.8 Flash rolling out three weeks after last release
snippet: After the last model release three weeks ago, Google today is rolling out Gemini 3.8 Flash. This marks the third Flash update in three months. more…
fullText:
After the last model release three weeks ago, Google today is rolling out Gemini 3.8 Flash. This marks the third Flash update in three months.

…our most intelligent workhorse model, delivering significant improvements from 3.7 Flash across software engineering, agentic tasks, and critical, multi-step reasoning in specialized domains.

Gemini 3.8 Flash “delivers substantial gains” over its predecessor in various benchmarks, with Google also noting how it is “often approaching the performance of higher-cost frontier models.”

On DeepSWE v1.1 (Long-Horizon Software Engineering) 3.8 Flash outperforms most larger frontier models in autonomously solving complex engineering problems end to end, only at a fraction of the cost.

In quantitative and professional fields that require advanced analysis and reporting, 3.8 Flash outperforms 3.7 Flash and other frontier models in benchmarks like Vals Finance Agent V2 and Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark. 

3.8 Flash also achieves a 54.9% on HLE-Verified, demonstrating its ability to handle multi-step reasoning across STEM, humanities, and professional fields.

Google says these “performance gains stem from a core design choice: 3.8 Flash works harder.”

On complex tasks, it exhibits greater diligence — executing extra reasoning steps, and calling tools iteratively. At times, the model might use more tokens to maximize performance, especially at higher effort levels.

Note: Updated DeepSWE v1.1 score

	

Similar to the previous model, Gemini 3.8 Flash’s knowledge cutoff date is March 2026 “for some domains while in others [users] may experience the model’s knowledge is limited to January 2025.”

Google is once again offering an introductory price of $0.75/1M input tokens and $3.75/1M output tokens until December 31.

Gemini 3.8 Flash is already live in the Gemini app for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers, AI Mode, and Gemini in Google Sheets. It’s also available for developers in Google Antigravity, AI Studio, and the Gemini API.

Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber

Google today also announced Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber (replacing 3.5) for trusted testers — via a new Fairwind Program — with “frontier-level performance in autonomous vulnerability discovery.”

The Chrome Security team found that 3.8 Flash Cyber produced 2.6 times more correct patches to vulnerabilities in Chrome than the best commercial models that are much larger.

Wiz found that Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber achieves +7.5-9.7% higher recall on their internal penetration testing benchmark for a 2.3-5.2x lower cost compared to other leading frontier models.

Google’s Cloud Vulnerability Research team leveraged the 3.8 Flash Cyber model to find a critical foundational vulnerability in less than 2 hours, a vulnerability for which research and discovery usually takes months.

title: Google stops selling ‘Certified Refurbished’ Pixel 7 series, still no Pixel 9 yet
snippet: Google has pulled refurbished Pixel 7 devices from its store, with the Pixel 9 yet to make its debut. more…
fullText:
Google has pulled refurbished Pixel 7 devices from its store, with the Pixel 9 yet to make its debut.

On the Google Store you can buy a “Certified Refurbished” Pixel smartphone at a lower price, usually hundreds off of the original retail price. While it’s not always the best deal compared to a used device on the private market, there’s considerable peace of mind in buying a refurbished device directly from Google seeing as every device comes with a one-year warranty, gets a full inspection with replacement parts, and is sold unlocked for use with any carrier. These devices are also available on Amazon.

But the options have now shrunk.

Google now only has the Pixel 8 series – 8, Pro, and 8a – available alongside the Pixel 7a, with prices ranging from $289 to $649. The Pixel 7 series has been removed in the past few days, with its final appearance on the Wayback Machine in late August. Google was running a promotion where refurbished Pixel 7 devices included a free Pixel Watch 2 from July up until the past week or so.

	

This doesn’t come as a huge surprise. The Pixel 7 series launched in 2022 and will stop getting updates in the latter half of 2027. What’s more of a surprise is that the Pixel 9 series has yet to arrive in Google’s refurbished program. With Pixel 11 now available, it’s likely the Pixel 9 will arrive in the coming weeks. Pixel 8 was added in October 2025, roughly two months after the Pixel 10’s debut.

title: Google Pixel adding ‘Battery usage summaries,’ rolling out on Pixel 10 and newer
snippet: Google is rolling out a new AI-generated feature on Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 devices called “Battery usage summaries” which translate battery use stats into natural language. more…
fullText:
Google is rolling out a new AI-generated feature on Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 devices called “Battery usage summaries” which translate battery use stats into natural language.

Rolling out via an AI Core update on Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 devices, “Battery usage summaries” deliver on a rather simple premise. On your battery usage page, a new AI-generated overview summarizes your battery usage, pulling in recent history and calling out more powerful apps. 

On a support page, Google explains:

At the top of the Battery usage page, you can get a personalized summary of your battery usage. It summarizes these analyses, which are performed in the background:

Identifies apps that consume the most battery.

Monitors app background activity.

Compares the overall and app-specific battery consumption between your selected period and recent average.

The feature is enabled by default on supported Pixels, but can be turned off via Settings > Battery & charging > Battery Usage > Battery usage summaries (overflow menu). A screenshot sent to Android Authority shows an example of what the summary might say beyond the “you’ve barely used your phone” vibes our unused-for-the-day Pixel 11 Pro Fold shows. Google says that “outputs vary and highlight the most important info only.”

	

Google’s support page mentions that the latest AI Core update is needed to enable the feature, but it’s unclear if there are any additional requirements. While we’re seeing the feature live on both a Pixel 11 Pro Fold and a Pixel 11 Pro XL, it’s not yet showing on Pixel 10 or Pixel 10a devices we’ve updated and tested.

If you’re seeing “Battery usage summaries” on your Pixel, let us know in the comments below.

title: FBI investigates as hackers sell digital scans of 153M drivers licenses
snippet: The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is reportedly investigating identity theft as digital scans of more than 153 million driver’s licenses went on sale on the dark web. Additional documents offered through a massive security breach include medical cards, residence cards, and more. The licenses belong to people in the US and Canada, and appear to have been collected by hacking an identity verification service … more…
fullText:
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is reportedly investigating identity theft as digital scans of more than 153 million driver’s licenses went on sale on the dark web. Additional documents offered through a massive security breach include medical cards, residence cards, and more.

The licenses belong to people in the US and Canada, and appear to have been collected by hacking an identity verification service … 

Krebs on Security was able to confirm the authenticity of the claim made by the cybercriminals as they were able to provide a scan of his own driving license, with other victims likewise confirming their scans were correct.

A new identity theft service [dubbed Nexus] launched on the dark web this week is selling digital scans of more than 153 million drivers licenses from people in the United States and Canada […] The people behind Nexus claim the license images are coming from an active breach at “a major identity verification company” whose customers include multiple Fortune 500 companies.

KrebsOnSecurity also has learned that the New Orleans field office of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) today launched an official inquiry into the source of the images.

The report says that the ID verification company appears to be one based in Louisiana. The criminals claim that they still have access to the source of these scans, a claim supported by their adding almost 400,000 new ones within the past 24 hours.

There are indications suggesting that at least some of the data was stolen from a verification service used by rental car company Hertz. The report points to a New Orleans-based company as a potential source, and that company’s client list includes Hertz, Target, Fedex, Motorola Solutions, Jack Henry, and Caesars Entertainment. There are many more details in the full report.

9to5Mac’s Take

The irony of criminals being able to hack an identity verification service in order to provide documents that can be used for identity theft would be amusing if it weren’t so serious. This type of breach is depressingly common.

It was recently estimated that online scams cost Americans almost $150 billion last year as the number of cyber scams continue to increase dramatically.

title: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026’s new Real World AI Stage features Nvidia, robots, and extinct animals
snippet: On our new Real World AI stage, we’ll be focusing on the intersection between the digital and physical, and all the ways we’ll continue to see a blending of the two.
fullText:
At our past TechCrunch Disrupt events, AI has taken center stage, both throughout our programming and in a stage of its own. This year, the technology, implications, and players are so rapidly developing and widespread that we’re expanding the single AI stage into two!

The AI Stage will continue as you’d expect, with a rundown of sessions and speakers available for review right here. But the Real World AI Stage is brand-new for TechCrunch Disrupt 2026.

On this stage, we’ll be focusing on that intersection between the digital and physical, and all the ways we’ll continue to see a blending of the two, as autonomous hardware goes beyond self-driving cars and enters public spaces, battlefields, our homes, and even potentially helps extinct species reenter Earth.

It’s a packed lineup featuring speakers from Shield AI, Colossal Biosciences, FieldAI, Foxglove, and more still to come. You can join in on all the excitement October 13 to 15 at San Francisco’s Moscone West, so register to attend right here.

But in the meantime, here’s the breakdown of our Real World AI Stage lineup:

Robots Are Waiting for Their ChatGPT Moment. Here Is What Is Standing in the Way

Large language models had the internet. Self-driving cars have millions of hours of road data. Robots have neither. That data gap is the single biggest reason most experts believe general-purpose robotic intelligence is still years away, despite the breakthroughs happening everywhere else in AI. A new wave of startups is racing to close it, building the data pipelines, simulation environments, and foundation models that could trigger the same capability explosion we saw with LLMs. This session asks the hard question: what does the ChatGPT moment for physical AI actually require, and how close are we really?

With Les Karpas, Head of Physical AI, Nvidia

Building AI Systems When Failure Is Not an Option 

When AI enters the physical world, the consequences of failure change. A mistake could lead to a grounded aircraft, a vehicle crash, or a compromised mission.

In this session, leaders who are building autonomous vehicles, defense technologies, and industrial systems will talk about one of the toughest questions that every hard tech founder must face: How do you know when your system is ready to be safely deployed?  

We’ll dig into how founders can create a safety culture, test and validate AI, navigate regulatory hurdles, and build companies that can earn trust when the stakes are high.   

With Nate Michael, CTO, Shield AI

Can We Engineer Nature’s Comeback? 

Ben Lamm has built one of the most controversial companies in tech by turning de-extinction from science fiction into a billion-dollar business. In this fireside chat, the Colossal Biosciences CEO will discuss the technologies used to revive extinct species, the role AI plays in modern biology, and the growing debate over whether engineering nature is a conservation breakthrough or a distraction from protecting what’s already here.

With Ben Lamm, CEO, Colossal Biosciences

Operating at the Edge: How AI Works When the Cloud Doesn’t 

The most valuable AI deployments in the world operate where the cloud can’t reach. And building for them requires a different technological playbook.  

This session brings together leaders from defense, space, and industrial AI who will share how they have tackled the challenge of making AI work at the edge — where latency matters, connectivity is limited, and failure isn’t an option. Expect practical lessons on architectural principles, design decisions, and trade-offs that make AI-centric systems work in the real world.   

With Dr. Ali Agha, CEO and founder of FieldAI; Michelle Lee, CEO and founder, Medra; and Aidan Madigan-Curtis, partner, Eclipse Ventures

From Prototype to Production: Can it scale in reality? 

A prototype that works is not a product. A product that ships is not a scaled business. The gap between each of those stages is where most deep tech startups die. Founders might have the right team and tech, but they fail to understand what it takes to bring a prototype into production and eventually scale to higher, profitable volumes.  

This session brings together founders who have crossed that gap in space hardware, humanoid robotics, and autonomous systems. They’ll share what they got wrong, what they’d do earlier, and what the prototype-to-production journey looks like when supply chains and manufacturing realities replace lab conditions.

With John Mackey, CEO, co-founder, MBRYONICS; Boris Sofman, co-founder and CEO, Bedrock Robotics; and Adrian Macneil, CEO, Foxglove

There’s plenty more in store for you at Disrupt 2026 — after all, that’s just one stage’s worth of programming! For a sense of what else you’ll get to access, we’ve also announced the:

Disrupt Stage, featuring top speakers from Replit, Amazon, Tether, and more.

AI Stage, digging into the security gaps and business model shifts AI is forcing on every SaaS company. 

Smart Money Stage, covering stablecoins, instant payments, and AI’s role in financial trust.

Smart Systems Stage, tackling the fusion breakthroughs and grid strain powering AI’s next decade. 

Builders Stage, where founders and investors get tactical about raising, hiring, and scaling.

Be part of Disrupt 2026 in San Francisco from October 13–15, where more than 10,000 startup, tech, and VC leaders come together for three days of insights, Startup Battlefield, unparalleled networking, and access to every stage and the exhibition floor.  

Register today!

title: OpenAI’s new reasoning technique alarms AI safety experts
snippet: OpenAI’s new Astra model will use “recurrent depth,” a technique that allows the model to operate outside of the sequential thinking that characterizes most reasoning models.
fullText:
OpenAI’s new Astra model will use a reasoning technique called “recurrent depth” that allows it to operate outside of the sequential thinking that characterizes most reasoning models, The Information reported on Tuesday. This technique, also called “opaque recurrence,” will likely make the model’s chain of thought more difficult to monitor — and that has AI safety experts rattled.

While Astra’s use of the technique is reportedly limited, its emergence has still raised significant concerns among AI safety experts.

“I am extremely concerned by the reporting that Astra uses opaque recurrence,” wrote Redwood CEO Buck Shlegeris in a post after the news broke. “I don’t know whether Astra is much less CoT monitorable than previous models. But if OpenAI pushes this technique further, they’ll have the option to massively increase the recurrence and totally destroys CoT monitorability.”

Longtime AI safety advocate Zvi Mowshowitz also weighed in and wrote that laws might be necessary to prevent a “race to the bottom” among AI labs. 

“The technique is playing with fire, risking a taboo that OpenAI and Anthropic have fought to establish that we work hard to maintain Chain of Thought faithfulness and monitorability for as long as we can,” Mowshowitz wrote. “More intensive use of such techniques would probably damage monitorability.”

Under normal circumstances, a reasoning model’s chain of thought provides the sequential steps taken by the model as it attempts to solve a problem. While the representation is imperfect, it still serves as a valuable tool for monitoring misbehavior or misalignment. In the case of OpenAI’s recent rogue agent activity, chain-of-thought records were an important tool in teasing out why agents behaved the way they did.

In opaque recurrence, the model takes a less linear approach, processing the same query several times in a loop. The result leaves fewer legible traces, effectively side-stepping a conventional chain-of-thought record.

Crucially, Astra’s use of the technique appears to be limited. The model’s chain of thought is still expected to be legible, and the company pushed back against any suggestion that it would shift to “neuralese.” OpenAI has already announced plans for extensive chain-of-thought monitoring systems as part of its forward-looking safety plans.

In a post on X, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki emphasized the lab’s commitment to legible chains of thought. “OpenAI has worked to preserve and utilize chain-of-thought monitoring since our very first reasoning models,” Pachocki wrote. “It’s a core goal of our current research program.

All AI models do some quantity of opaque reasoning, and few researchers take chain-of-thought logs as a direct representation of a model’s reasoning. Still, those caveats don’t dispel the concern that opaque recurrence may make AI reasoning harder to monitor, particularly as it grows in use across different models. In a follow-up report Wednesday morning, The Information reported that both Anthropic and Google DeepMind were already discussing the technique.

In a post responding to the news, Redwood Research chief scientist Ryan Greenblatt said opaque reasoning could easily scale faster than conventional chain-of-thought reasoning, effectively removing all reasoning from visible channels.

“My biggest concern is that a natural progression from here would involve scaling up the opaque reasoning to the point where the model reasons entirely or almost entirely in latent space,” Greenblatt wrote. “I hope it isn’t too late to avoid the most concerning architectures and that OpenAI will stop here.”

fullText:
Apple surprised many when it quietly announced updated Mac mini and Mac Studio models shortly before its September event. We would normally have expected these announcements to be part of that event.

One strong theory is that the company may be making a lot of big announcements in its ‘Surprise and shine‘ keynote, and therefore wanted to get these updates out of the way beforehand. But a new report presents another theory … 

Announcing the new Mac mini and Mac Studio models just a fortnight ahead of the September 9th event seemed surprising. Why not wait the extra couple of weeks and do it properly, rather than just via press releases?

The Information says that the decision was made because the company was taken by surprise by the level of demand for the models for AI applications, and with some configurations unavailable for months, Apple brought the announcements forward for this reason.

9to5Mac’s Take

There’s certainly no doubt that the power of Apple Silicon has made both the Mac mini and Mac Studio popular options for those wanting to run AI models locally. For example, we’ve seen researchers use Thunderbolt 5 to turn four Mac Studios into an extremely powerful AI cluster.

I can also believe that Apple did not initially predict the scale of demand this was going to generate.

What seems less likely, however, is the idea that two weeks makes any worthwhile difference to the situation. To me, it’s just too small a gap for this to be a credible explanation. Personally, I think the existing theory we outlined is the more likely one.

Apple will want to make a very big fuss about the launch of its first foldable iPhone and also ensure that the iPhone 18 Pro isn’t seen as an also-ran. If Apple does indeed unveil the HomePad smart home hub as we expect, that too will be a major announcement.

We then need to add in a new Apple TV and HomePod mini 2 – both with Siri AI capabilities – two new Apple Watch models, and potentially new AirPods too. That’s a lot of announcements for a single keynote, so I could absolutely understand wanting to launch the new Mac desktops beforehand.

title: Android 17 boosts network security by hiding domain names, lets carriers disable 2G
snippet: Google is out with a blog post today recapping new network security measures in Android 17. more…
fullText:
Google is out with a blog post today recapping new network security measures in Android 17.

Even with HTTPS connections, the domain names of websites (including apps) are “still visible to network operators and eavesdroppers.” 

This unencrypted data can be used to build user profiles or, in the hands of malicious actors, leveraged for targeted phishing and scam campaigns.

Android 17 aims to resolve this with Encrypted Client Hello (ECH). Working with private DNS, this new privacy standard will “obscure the domain names you visit.” This works by hiding the “domain name using a secret encryption key that only the destination website can unscramble.”

By encrypting the destination website name from the very start, ECH helps ensure that, for supported websites and apps, network providers and network snoopers can no longer easily see which websites or apps you are accessing.

With OS support now available, app developers have to upgrade to OkHttp 5.5.0 and enable ECH.

	

Domain name data leaks in two places, (1) the initial DNS lookup and (2) the unencrypted ClientHello in the Transport Layer Security (TLS) handshake. Recent progress with the rollout of encrypted DNS and the launch of support for Encrypted ClientHello on Android 17 are helping to make online activity more private

On the network front, Android 17 allows mobile carriers to turn off 2G connectivity by default for their users. (Android 12 first introduced this user setting.) This is intended to counter SMS blaster attacks that “force nearby smartphones to drop their LTE or 5G connections and downgrade to less secure, legacy 2G networks.” Phishing texts are then sent to devices.

Meanwhile, Android 17 enforces Local Network Protection wherein apps must now request permission “before they can scan or connect to other devices on your local network.”

For everyday tasks like casting a video to your TV, developers should adopt a secure system tool, which allows you to select your TV without the app ever needing permission to see the other devices in your home.

Finally, Certificate Transparency requires “all certificates to be logged in a public registry, making such an attack much less likely to go unnoticed.”

When you connect to a secure app or website, your device verifies a certificate to confirm the site is authentic. However, if a certificate issuer is compromised, hackers could potentially create fake certificates to intercept your traffic and cause harm.

title: Trump Administration Sides With OpenAI in Publishers’ Copyright Lawsuits
snippet: The federal government says making AI companies pay for content used to train their models would undermine national security.
fullText:
The Trump administration has weighed in on a series of copyright disputes between news organizations and OpenAI, supporting the ChatGPT-maker’s position that its use of publishers’ content to train AI models constituted fair use.

The statement of interest of the United States (PDF) was filed Tuesday in a series of cases in the US District Court for the Southern District of New York, including one initiated by The New York Times and another by Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company. Ziff Davis filed the suit in 2025, alleging OpenAI infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.

In its filing, the federal government said a ruling in publishers’ favor could hinder AI development, limit competition among AI firms and hurt the country’s competitiveness with foreign developers.

“Rules of law that make it significantly more difficult to develop a robust AI industry in the United States … threaten national security and give a competitive advantage to foreign adversaries who are not so encumbered,” the filing states.

Graham James, a spokesperson for The New York Times, told CNET in a statement that the administration is “siding with a handful of trillion-dollar AI companies” instead of American creators and that doing so undermines both creators and AI developers.

“Both AI and creators can thrive – AI companies simply need to pay fairly for the content that makes their products possible, as copyright law requires,” James said. “The Administration’s proposal to let companies take that content without permission or compensation would undermine the sustainability of the human-created content that a healthy society depends on, and which AI needs to function.”

CNET has reached out to representatives for OpenAI and Ziff Davis for comment. 

The Times initiated the lawsuit at the end of 2023, a year after ChatGPT’s debut. In its initial complaint (PDF), the news organization said large language models, such as those that power ChatGPT, were built using content that included millions of its articles. That training constituted an effort to “free-ride” on the Times’ investment in journalism and create products that compete.

The government said it sees LLMs’ ability to help others compete with large media corporations as a positive development. It cited independent authors using AI models to generate images that might otherwise require a photographer or license, and LLMs directing users to “dissenting sources that offer contrary information or perspectives.”

“It is not in the public’s interest for the largest technology companies to have an oligopoly on LLM training due to licensing entry barriers that function primarily as large subsidies for old mainstream media companies,” the government stated.

Major media companies aren’t the only ones who’ve sued OpenAI over copyright infringement. Authors, including big names like George R.R. Martin, have also accused the company of using their works in model training. OpenAI rival Anthropic, which makes Claude, settled piracy claims with authors for $1.5 billion, although a judge ruled the company’s use of copyrighted material was fair use. 

Earlier this summer, publishers accused OpenAI of withholding evidence about how it trains its models, claims the company has denied.

snippet: iPhone 18 Pro is launching next week, and expected to feature three upgrades that have been rumored for years. Here’s what’s coming. more…
fullText:
iPhone 18 Pro is launching next week, and expected to feature three upgrades that have been rumored for years. Here’s what’s coming.

#1: Variable aperture camera

It’s been more than two years since The Information published a report detailing a “variable aperture” camera system coming to iPhone. At the time, it claimed iPhone 17 was the target model for the new feature. Ming Chi-Kuo, however, chimed in that it was instead set for the iPhone 18 line.

Now, iPhone 18 Pro is almost here and the latest reporting indicates variable aperture is indeed coming to the Main camera—at least on Pro Max, if not both models.

The new feature could unlock a variety of exciting camera abilities, but it all depends on Apple’s implementation. Fortunately we’re just days away from the unveiling and full feature reveal.

#2: Smaller Dynamic Island

It’s been almost 10 years since the iPhone X introduced the notch, the first cutout in an iPhone display. It wasn’t until 2022’s iPhone 14 Pro that the current Dynamic Island design arrived, shrinking the cutout.

Now four years later, a smaller Dynamic Island is finally coming with iPhone 18 Pro.

Rumors indicate Apple’s new Dynamic Island cutout will be about 35% smaller than the previous design. This reduction in size is even hinted at by Siri’s new look in iOS 27.

#3: Apple-designed C2 modem

Apple’s in-house modem efforts have been an open secret for years. But it was just last year that the first Apple-designed modem launched in an iPhone: the C1.

	

Now, rumors indicate Apple plans to switch away from Qualcomm modems in iPhone 18 Pro in favor of its own next-gen C2 chip.

C2 will likely bring speed gains over C1X and C1, but it’s also expected to boast the improved efficiency and privacy benefits of every Apple-designed modem.

title: Qualcomm’s upcoming premium chip has Adreno ‘Neural Fusion’ GPU
snippet: Following Qualcomm detailing the core Oryon CPU that would find itself on the next flagship Snapdragon chip, the chipmaker has announced its next-gen Adreno Neural Fusion GPU. more…
fullText:
Following Qualcomm detailing the core Oryon CPU that would find itself on the next flagship Snapdragon chip, the chipmaker has announced its next-gen Adreno Neural Fusion GPU.

Qualcomm’s next SoC will be the first chipset to feature dedicated AI GPU cores in the graphics pipeline. These so-called “Matrix Cores” sit snugly in each of the three 1.45GHz GPU slices on the new Adreno GPU. Qualcomm says they act as dedicated local hardware to “run advanced AI models directly inside the graphics pipeline.”

The Snapdragon chip’s Adreno GPU will also feature a dedicated 18MB HPM (High Performance Memory) cache. That capacity sounds humble, but Qualcomm says its HPM “provides large, low-latency memory directly to the GPU, allowing tile-based rendering,

frame buffers, and compute workloads to remain local to the graphics subsystem.”

Both components in the new core architecture help make up the entirety of the Adreno Neural Fusion GPU. For the end user, it means a 40% power improvement with the technology enabled. The company detailed in its press release how developing an SoC with AI processing done in closer proximity to the GPU means less latency and better efficiency.

	

The trick is keeping the work close to the silicon. Adreno Matrix Cores handle AI models right where the graphics happen, and the 18MB of Adreno High Performance Memory holds the heavy data—tiles, frame buffers, compute—on-chip so it isn’t constantly shuffling back and forth to system memory. Less movement means lower latency and better efficiency, which translates into gaming sessions that last longer.

For the time being, Unity and Unreal Engine have already integrated Qualcomm’s Neural Fusion stack.

The end result should be improved graphics quality with “upscaled images, stable frame rates, and improved efficiency through AI-enhanced rendering built directly into the Snapdragon

graphics pipeline,” as Qualcomm puts it.

Snapdragon Summit is scheduled for September 22-24, and more is set to be announced regarding the new chip’s NPU.

title: Adobe brings Photoshop, Firefly, and 70+ creative tools to Slack with MCP app
snippet: Adobe is bringing its creative and productivity tools directly into Slack, letting teams create and edit images, videos, designs and PDFs without leaving the conversations where projects already take shape. more…
fullText:
Adobe is bringing its creative and productivity tools directly into Slack, letting teams create and edit images, videos, designs and PDFs without leaving the conversations where projects already take shape.

Slackbot gains access to Photoshop, Firefly, Acrobat, and more

The new Adobe for Slack MCP app launches today with more than 70 pro-grade tools spanning Firefly, Adobe Express, Photoshop, Premiere, Acrobat, InDesign, Illustrator, Stock, Lightroom and more.

It works through Slackbot, Slack’s built-in AI assistant. Slackbot can pull context from messages, files, channels and Canvases before calling the appropriate Adobe tools.

Context is the heart of the integration. A user could ask Slackbot to summarize a project brief, then turn the information into a PDF, image or video.

The app can also search Creative Cloud assets by subject, style or mood and bring the results into a Slack workflow for further editing.

Other examples include resizing approved campaign creative for different social platforms, transforming spreadsheet data into a shareable visual and refining batches of photos.

Adobe says users can remove backgrounds and distractions, adjust lighting and tone, crop images and produce multiple variations from Slack.

Availability 

Adobe for Slack is available globally to Slack Business+ and Enterprise+ customers across desktop, web and mobile starting today.

People can start without an Adobe account, while signing in unlocks more tools, generative AI features, Creative Cloud files and continuity across sessions.

The launch expands Adobe’s push to bring its tools into AI chatbots. Adobe already supports ChatGPT, Claude and Copilot, with Gemini integration coming soon.

You can learn more in Adobe’s announcement.

title: Mammotion Luba 3 changed my mind about robot lawnmowers
snippet: Robot lawnmowers have long intrigued me, but I never really wanted one. After a few weeks with the Mammotion Luba 3, though, I’m sold, because this fixed my biggest issue with other models. more…
fullText:
Robot lawnmowers have long intrigued me, but I never really wanted one. After a few weeks with the Mammotion Luba 3, though, I’m sold, because this fixed my biggest issue with other models.

I’m all for smart home advancements, but a robot lawnmower was one I was never really a fan of. I like mowing my lawn, crazy as that sounds, and leaving that to a robot felt like more set up and maintain than it was going to be worth. Inevitably, though, curiosity won over. When Mammotion sent over the Luba 3 AWD mower, my attitude flipped.

The main reason for that boils down to how this mower operates. Unlike many others, which require the use of a boundary perimeter or RTK base station, the Mammotion Luba 3 operates with what’s called a “NetRTK,” which is effectively just a highly accurate satellite positioning system combined with LiDAR.

The results here really blew me away. 

	

After mapping the robot to the areas of my yard I wanted it to work on, it stayed nearly perfectly within those lines, to the point where I actually had to go back and redo the lines. Initially, I’d set up several feet of buffer zone between the mower and the fairly-busy road in front of my lawn for fear that, if the positioning shifted, the mower might risk getting run over. The first two runs showed how misplaced that fear was. It hit its lines almost perfectly, which left plenty of room for me to adjust those lines much closer to the road. There’s still a small buffer, but I now know I can trust that Luba 3 isn’t going to go rogue into the road. It’s not without hiccups. Another part of the yard with a ditch left the mower stuck a couple of times when the positioning was off by a few inches, and a tough-to-access area of the property also proved tricky. But in most cases, it goes off without a hitch.

It’s all managed through the app, where you use a virtual joystick to set up a map and the pathways the mower can use to get to various zones, including crossing over driveways or perhaps portions of your neighbor’s lawn. The same app can be used to set schedules, view progress, and even watch a first-person-view of the mower’s main camera as it runs through your yard.

Taking a step back, the initial setup is an absolute breeze. Assembly and setup took around 30 minutes, with the included tools making it easy to attach the front bumper and side covers. 

Luba 3 has a docking station in the box that just needs a power outlet in the vicinity, with a generous length of cable included. You want a fairly level location for this, but I’ve found that even my slightly uneven and unstable mulch base works well enough. I’ve only had one occasion where it didn’t fully seat for charging in several weeks of use. You do get a physical RTK base station in the box but, really, you don’t need it unless you’re in some very specific circumstances. 

Like most robot mowers, grass is cut using some fairly small blades underneath, and this also makes the whole thing feel safer. Not only is there a giant “STOP” button at the top, but the blades themselves won’t be able to do nearly as much damage as a real mower would.

The physical hardware is huge, easily 2-3x the size of a robot vacuum, and it turns heads. My dogs still go crazy every time they see this in the yard, and I always see neighbors and drivers passing by turn to look when Luba 3 is out in the front. But it’s not an eyesore either. The white finish shows all dirt and dust that’s kicked up – most of the pictures in this post are after about two weeks without a wipedown – but it’s a sensible color choice as it rejects heat. It is heavy at 41lbs, but that’s totally managable for the rare occasions where you need to move it manually.

How’s the actual mowing performance? 

Good, but not perfect.

Luba 3 thankfully cuts at up to 3.9-inches in height, which matters to me. Overly short grass is how you kill a lawn in a hot summer, so it was nice to see Mammotion offers the right amount of height to keep everything fairly healthy. Whether sending it off into a thick lawn or one that’s mostly been scorched by the heat and drought of the North Carolina summer I’ve been living in, Luba 3 gets the job done well. The cut is fairly even with only the occasional straggler blade left behind, particularly when cutting at maximum height or when running it less frequently. This benefits great from running on a regular basis rather than the “as needed” schedule you’d use with a traditional mower.

It also handles slopes like a champ, with it able to cover my steep front lawn and some other raised portions of the yard without skipping a beat. Mammotion says it can handle a slope of up to 38.6-degrees with its all-wheel-drive setup. There are a couple of spots in my lawn where I can tell there’s some dead grass from Luba’s tracks, but I’ll mostly blame that on the local conditions. In some particularly uneven parts of my lawn, I do need to go back with my push mower or weed-eater, but Luba 3 really takes the bulk of the work off of my plate – complete with stripes in the finished yard.

I do think that’s an important note to make. Mammotion’s Luba 3, and really any robot lawnmower, isn’t going to fully end your yard work. There are certain sections you’ll need to do yourself, especially with regard to weeds and edging along the sides. There are options that aim to solve this, but you’ll still inevitably need to do cleanup here and there. 

But most weeks, this cuts my mowing time from an hour or two to just a few minutes – a couple of passes along the road, checking for spots it might have missed, and then weed-eating around the driveway and fence.

As for battery life, the 0.75-acre model I’ve been testing can run for about two hours before it takes a break to recharge, but that’s largely due to the hills it has to deal with. Mammotion says that, under ideal conditions, it can run for up to 215 minutes (about 3.5 hours).

Another point in favor of its navigation, too, is that it can easily handle jumping around to different portions of the yard. Zones are easy to set up and can make it easy to mow different areas at different times, or juggle things like fences. Part of my yard is gated, so having a specific zone I can run just when the gate is open is a really handy option.

All-in-all, Mammotion really changed my mind about robot lawnmowers. Luba 3 works like a charm and addresses every complaint I thought I’d have about setup, navigation, and cutting performance. 

Really, the only tough part left is price.

Mammotion Luba 3 AWD starts at $2,399 in the US, which is not cheap. But this is also on the bleeding edge and, in a world where time is money, might be worthwhile for anyone who just can’t seem to keep up with their lawn. It saves so much time.

fullText:
Anker’s new robot lawnmower might take over for your weedwacker, too. Announced at IFA 2026, the Eufy Robot Lawn Mower S2 Max comes with an extendable trimming arm to clean up the grass around your driveway and flowerbeds.

The dual-blade mower offers vSLAM navigation that uses built-in cameras to build a 3D map of your yard, eliminating the need to set up boundary wires or a Real-Time Kinematic (RTK) base station. Anker says the Mower S2 Max can map and mow up to 3.7 acres, while handling yards with up to 80 percent (38-degree) slopes. The robot mower is AWD and will launch in May 2027 for €3,999. There’s no word on US pricing or availability yet.

1/3The Eufy Robot Lawn Mower S2 Max. Image: Anker

As built-in edgers crop up in robot mower models from Segway, Ecovacs, Roborock, and now Anker, even Mammotion is jumping on the bandwagon with the newly announced Luba 4 AWD, which uses an edge-cutting attachment to trim against walls, fences, and garden borders.

The Mammotion Luba 4 AWD roves your yard using four cameras on the front, sides, and rear of the device, along with a 360-degree LiDAR system and network RTK, which taps into the cloud for navigation. Mammotion says the three-sensor system helps to ensure “zero dead zones and zero drift.” Additionally, the Luba 4 AWD comes with independent front-wheel steering, helping the mower change directions without U-turns that might leave tracks on your yard.

1/5The Luba 4 AWD. Image: Mammotion

The Luba 4 AWD is available in three models, with the 3000F cutting up to 0.75 acres and the 6000F handling up to 1.5 acres. The 12000F is designed to cut up to 3 acres, but it doesn’t support the edge-trimming attachment. The dual-disc system on the 3000F and 6000F models supports a wider 17.3-inch cutting width, while the three cutting discs on the 12000F span 20.9 inches. Mammotion plans to open preorders for the Luba 4 AWD later this year, but it hasn’t shared details on pricing yet.

snippet: Today is John Ternus’s first day as Apple CEO. A new Bloomberg report has more details on other executive changes, plus tidbits on changes Ternus might make. more…
fullText:
Today is John Ternus’s first day as Apple CEO. A new Bloomberg report has more details on other executive changes, plus tidbits on changes Ternus might make.

Luca Maestri

Bloomberg reports that Luca Maestri is stepping down as Apple’s “Corporate Services” leader. Maestri served as Apple CFO until January 2025, when he stepped down to take on a smaller role. As head of Corporate Services, Maestri oversaw information systems and technology, information security, and real estate and development.

According to today’s report, Maestri left that job “in recent weeks.” He is, however, still on Apple’s payroll. His only remaining responsibility is “hosting a popular class at Apple University, an in-house program for teaching Apple’s ways to rising executives and employees.”

Bloomberg says that Maestri’s Corporate Services tasks have been shifted to CFO Kevan Parekh.

Adrian Perica

Mark Gurman points out that Apple’s new Leadership page excludes Adrian Perica, its head of mergers and acquisitions.

Apple’s new leadership page also excludes Adrian Perica, the company’s head of mergers and acquisitions. It remains unclear where he will shift within Apple. Bloomberg reported on Sunday that he would likely be dropped by Ternus as a direct report and could split his responsibilities across Apple’s services and finance teams.

It’s possible this signals a change to Apple’s strategy for mergers and acquisitions. Some analysts expect Ternus to be more aggressive in making bigger acquisitions.

A change to how Apple manages outgoing executives

Gurman also says that “people in and around Apple” expect Ternus to change how the company handles outgoing executives. While Cook made a habit of retaining executives in smaller roles, like Maestri, Gurman says “Ternus may be less likely to continue using this approach.”

More tidbits

Ternus officially joined X today, and his first tweet was an all-lowercase “hello” with no punctuation. The post was quoted by marketing exec Greg Joswiak, who wrote: “Hello, indeed. More to say September 9.”

Gurman says Apple is hosting an event at Apple Park today “to introduce John Ternus as its new CEO to employees and to again celebrate Tim Cook’s tenure.”

Laura Legros, a former Apple VP who Ternus recruited out of retirement last month, will reportedly serve in a “Chief of Staff” style role. Cook did not have a person like this around him, according to Gurman.

title: Meta launches Muse Voice Transcribe for real-time voice dictation on Mac
snippet: Meta is launching Muse Voice Transcribe, its first real-time audio perception model. It brings multilingual, streaming transcription to Meta AI for Mac, Muse Code, and developers through the Meta Model API. more…
fullText:
Meta is launching Muse Voice Transcribe, its first real-time audio perception model. It brings multilingual, streaming transcription to Meta AI for Mac, Muse Code, and developers through the Meta Model API.

Muse Voice Transcribe powers system-wide dictation on Mac

Meta Superintelligence Labs says Muse Voice Transcribe combines streaming automatic speech recognition with speaker diarization and endpointing.

In practical terms, it can transcribe speech as it happens, separate speakers across recordings with 20-plus voices, and determine when someone has finished talking, all without a separate post-processing step.

The model was trained across more than 70 languages, with 25 validated at launch. It supports audio longer than an hour, plus native code-switching within or between sentences. Language, keyword, and context biasing can further improve recognition.

Rather than using one fixed tradeoff between speed and accuracy, Muse Voice Transcribe decides how long to listen before committing each word. Meta calls this “adaptive delay.” The system can move quickly through easier speech while using more audio context for difficult words.

Meta says the model ranks first on the Artificial Analysis streaming speech-to-text leaderboard as of September 1.

Muse Voice Transcribe is available today through the Meta Model API for $3 per 1,000 audio-minutes, equivalent to $0.18 per hour. 

It is also already powering dictation in Meta AI for Mac and Muse Code. On Mac, users can hold the Fn key to dictate into any application.

Introducing Muse Voice Transcribe! 🗣️

This is our first real-time audio perception model from @AIatMeta. It's trained on 70+ languages and delivers diarization with 20+ speakers. A truly fantastic model.

Available now in the Meta AI macOS app! pic.twitter.com/HMAj0i2o5q

title: Sonos unveils ‘Sonos 27’ software with four new features
snippet: Today alongside launching two new products, Sonos has unveiled ‘Sonos 27’ branding for its software platform and detailed four new features coming soon for Sonos users. more…
fullText:
Today alongside launching two new products, Sonos has unveiled ‘Sonos 27’ branding for its software platform and detailed four new features coming soon for Sonos users.

Here are four new ‘Sonos 27’ features launching this fall

Sonos has launched Sonos Ace Ultra headphones today alongside a Sonos Beam Ultra soundbar. And in addition to the new hardware introductions, the company has rebranded its software.

‘Sonos 27’ is the official name of the Sonos software platform that already exists, but is getting a proper name starting today. More than just a rebrand though, Sonos announced four new software features coming this fall to Sonos users:

Portable surrounds

Personal listening

Sonos 27voice

Sonos MCP

Portable surrounds

Turn two compatible portable speakers into wireless rear surrounds for movie night — then move them right back to wherever they usually live when the credits roll. No wires, no permanent setup, no rearranging furniture.

Personal listening, without missing a beat

Headphone linking which is available in Early Access, allows you to seamlessly move audio between Sonos Ace Ultra and a compatible Sonos speaker or group streaming over the same WiFi connection with just the press of a button. You will also be able to pick and control your music on your headphones directly in the Sonos app while on your home network. For more information, read our support article here.

The new Sonos voice experience

Sonos 27voice is a new way to ask for music, built specifically for that purpose in the home, and the shortest path from wanting a song to hearing it. Instead of remembering exact commands, you can ask the way you’d talk to someone in the room with you. Say things like “Play that song I had on in the kitchen last night,” or “Put on something downstairs that the kids will like.” The system works out the rest.

Control Sonos with the AI you already use

Sonos has always been an open platform. Sonos MCP expands it. Sonos MCP connects your system to frontier large language models (LLMs), so you can control Sonos from familiar chatbot interfaces and mix advanced dialog and reasoning with out-loud listening on your speakers.

You can find full details on these new Sonos 27 features, including specific availability and early access, on Sonos’ website.

title: Pixel 11 Pro bug causing static sounds in recordings while using Video Boost, fix coming [U]
snippet: Google continues to improve on video quality with each new Pixel release, but a bug on the Pixel 11 Pro series causes static audio issues when using the Video Boost feature. more…
fullText:
Google continues to improve on video quality with each new Pixel release, but a bug on the Pixel 11 Pro series causes static audio issues when using the Video Boost feature.

Update 9/1: In a statement, Google says that a fix is officially coming for this problem and will roll out via a Camera app update “in the coming weeks.”

We have identified the cause and developed a software fix that will rollout to users in the coming weeks via the Camera app. Additionally, further performance optimizations will be included in an upcoming monthly Android update.

Video Boost first launched on the Pixel 8 Pro back in 2023, delivering major improvements to video quality after adding in some powerful cloud processing. The feature works by uploading your footage to Google’s servers where advanced models can improve the quality quite drastically. It’s still a Pro-only feature, though.

On Pixel 11 devices, though, there’s a problem with static audio when using Video Boost.

	

Users noticed the problem last week and the reports just keep coming in. A video shared on Reddit shows the problem clearly, with static bursts every few seconds during the recording. It’s very obvious and almost sounds like a Bluetooth device that’s just at the edge of its range. Several have chimed in on the thread saying they’ve run into the exact same issue.  

A potential temporary fix for this seems to be clearing the cache on the Google Camera app and/or turning off Audio Zoom, but it sounds like Google is aware of the problem.

Let us know in the comments below if you’re running into these static burst noises on Pixel 11 Pro videos.

title: John Ternus just revealed his priorities in first introduction as Apple CEO
snippet: John Ternus is officially Apple’s CEO starting today, and his new bio page on Apple’s website reveals some of Ternus’s key priorities, as noted by Myke Hurley. more…
fullText:
John Ternus is officially Apple’s CEO starting today, and his new bio page on Apple’s website reveals some of Ternus’s key priorities, as noted by Myke Hurley.

John Ternus’s new Apple bio signals his priorities on day one as CEO

Today Apple updated its leadership page with John Ternus’s new title as CEO.

Alongside the leadership refresh, Ternus’s official bio has been updated and expanded too.

As noted by Myke Hurley at The Enthusiast, the new bio highlights three key narratives around Ternus’s time at Apple and the work that he cares deeply about. And two of those narratives are based on an all-new bio addition.

While the bio partly carries over details that were there before, there’s one brand new paragraph quoted below. From Apple’s website:

John has led much of the company’s focus in areas like reliability and durability, introducing new techniques that have made Apple products remarkably resilient. He has also driven much of Apple’s innovation in materials and hardware design that have reduced the carbon footprint of its products, including the creation of a new recycled aluminum compound that has been introduced across multiple product lines, the use of 3D-printed titanium in Apple Watch Ultra, and advancements in reparability that have increased the life spans of several Apple products.

This is the only entirely new paragraph. The rest of the bio either remains the same as before, or has been reworded but with the core message unchanged.

The new paragraph takes up nearly half the length of the whole bio, which is relatively brief overall.

As a result, this one paragraph is a strong indicator of priorities that matter a lot to Ternus, and that he wants to specifically highlight as he starts his CEO role.

To sum up the paragraph, Ternus cares about hardware “reliability and durability,” and “innovation in materials and hardware design,” with the goal of a reduced carbon footprint and increased product lifespans.

We’re seen a big emphasis from Tim Cook on reducing Apple’s carbon footprint. Ternus is clearly signaling that will continue under his leadership. But this paragraph also emphasizes that Ternus is an innovator in hardware design, and aims to create products that last for many years.

What are your takeaways from John Ternus’s new CEO bio? Let us know in the comments.
