title: YouTube overhauls its app-to-TV experience, shared Wi-Fi network no longer required
snippet: Casting from YouTube to your television has been a thing since, well, since Google first rolled out its Cast protocol well over a decade ago, and though the site’s default TV interface is pretty good these days, casting remains the preference of Chromecast veterans everywhere. If you count yourself among that crowd, good news: Google is overhauling how the app-to-TV experience works with YouTube. more…
fullText:
Casting from YouTube to your television has been a thing since, well, since Google first rolled out its Cast protocol well over a decade ago, and though the site’s default TV interface is pretty good these days, casting remains the preference of Chromecast veterans everywhere. If you count yourself among that crowd, good news: Google is overhauling how the app-to-TV experience works with YouTube.

As described in an announcement post on the YouTube support forums, Google is rolling out some big changes to how YouTube on your smartphone interacts with your television. The company is describing your device as a “companion” now, even ditching the classic Cast icon for something a little more generic. It’s a change that, based on Reddit threads, seemingly entered testing earlier in 2026, and is now ready for a full rollout. 

It’s not just a new way to describe pairing your devices, though. With this refresh, casting videos from your phone to a television now sounds like it has a whole lot less friction, thanks in part to a shift on completely relying on account-based management. These changes include:

No longer requiring both devices to be on a shared Wi-Fi network to cast. Instead, users will need to be signed in on the same account on both devices.

The ability to like videos, leave comments, and subscribe to channels while the video plays in the background.

The option to consume YouTube Shorts content on your phone while a different, full-length video plays on your television.

A built-in “Play on different device” option found within the menu button on every video listed in your homepage feed.

There are, of course, some caveats to these upgrades, and it primarily revolves around the shift to forcing account-based pairing between devices. While this should work wonders for private viewing sessions — i.e., casting a video from your own phone to your own television to watch either independently or with someone else in the room — it’s unclear if this completely removes the ability to cast over Wi-Fi, something that’s genuinely useful in larger gatherings with multiple participants. That’s a pretty common use case for watching YouTube on a television, so I’m hoping generic Cast support continues to exist in this format. Otherwise, this feels like a particularly anti-social change from Google.

	

Generally, though, these are all steps in the right direction, taking a lot of the existing Cast elements and simply streamlining them for a more modern second-screen experience. That “Play on different device” option, for example, appears to be pretty similar to the current casting menu, but won’t require you to begin playing a video on your phone prior to beaming it to your TV. Personally, browsing Shorts while watching a full-length video on your television sounds pretty overwhelming to me, but it’s certainly Google meeting modern viewers where they’re already at.

Today’s announcement did not include a specific rollout window, but it does sound like it’ll be coming to a mobile device near you very, very soon.

title: Anthropic upgrades Claude with new Fable 5.1 model, details here
snippet: In June, Anthropic first released Fable 5, its Mythos-class AI model for Claude. Three months later, Anthropic is enhancing Claude with its new Fable 5.1 model upgrade. more…
fullText:
In June, Anthropic first released Fable 5, its Mythos-class AI model for Claude. Three months later, Anthropic is enhancing Claude with its new Fable 5.1 model upgrade.

Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 arrive today

In Anthropic’s world, Fable is Claude’s most capable model. Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus are the small, medium, and large models below Fable. 

“Claude Fable 5.1 sets a new standard on coding, knowledge work, and long-running problem-solving tasks,” Anthropic says. The company says the new model has a higher level of performance compared to Fable 5.

Anthropic also says Fable 5.1 “achieves similar or better results than Fable 5 at a much lower cost” when set to low or medium effort.

More from Anthropic below:

Fable 5.1 avoids shortcuts that result in poorer-quality work, and it’s smart enough to fix the root causes of software issues. For example, in testing by the investment firm Millennium, Fable 5.1 found the cause of a rare crash on their internal systems that none of their engineers (or any other model) had been able to explain after several years of trying.

In addition to Fable 5.1, Anthropic is also releasing Mythos 5.1 for users with Mythos access.

“Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1 are the same model, but with different levels of safeguards,” Anthropic explains. “Fable 5.1 is generally available, while Mythos 5.1 is available only through our trusted access programs; its safeguards are specifically designed to support work in cybersecurity and the life sciences.”

Here’s pricing data for Fable 5.1:

Fable 5.1 will cost an estimated 25% less than Fable 5 for typical workloads, wherever usage is billed by token. This is because we’re reducing our pricing on cache reads (where the model reads inputs that have already been processed and stored). For highly agentic work, the savings will often be much larger—up to approximately 45%.

In terms of pricing, Anthropic says it has “reduced the price of Fable 5.1’s cache reads (where the model reuses context it has already processed) wherever usage is billed by token, such as on our API.” The company says this “leads to a substantial reduction in the overall cost of running the model.” Pricing is otherwise unchanged from Fable 5.

You can learn much more in the announcement post here.

title: iOS 27 fixes Apple Mail in three ways longtime users will love
snippet: iOS 27 is packed with powerful features like Siri AI and upgrades to productivity apps like Apple Mail, Notes, Reminders, and Calendar. But for many users, some of iOS 27’s best changes might be bug fixes that make apps run better than ever—here are three coming to Apple Mail. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 is packed with powerful features like Siri AI and upgrades to productivity apps like Apple Mail, Notes, Reminders, and Calendar. But for many users, some of iOS 27’s best changes might be bug fixes that make apps run better than ever—here are three coming to Apple Mail.

Apple Mail in iOS 27 has improved badge accuracy, faster message loading, and more reliable search

There’s no shortage of new features in iOS 27. But Apple also took extra time with this update to make everything run smoother and more reliably than before.

It’s not often the company touts bug fixes as a feature, but that’s exactly what happened when iOS 27 was announced.

Among iOS 27’s quality-of-life improvements, there are three Apple Mail fixes that longtime users should appreciate:

Improved unread badge accuracy

Faster message loading

More reliable search indexing

These three improvements were highlighted on a massive slide containing hundreds of big and small iOS 27 changes. 

Unread badge accuracy has been a personal pet peeve of mine for years. I keep badges disabled for most apps, but of those precious few where they’re enabled, Mail has been a top offender in showing a phantom badge or inaccurate number.

It’s similarly frustrating when messages in the inbox take too long to open, but Apple has sped up message loading in iOS 27.

	

And while your mileage may vary, I’ve found iOS 27‘s search improvements in Mail a noticeable upgrade.

These bug fixes join the handful of new features for Apple Mail in iOS 27. So if you haven’t used Mail in a while, iOS 27 could be a great time to revisit it.

title: TCL’s latest NXTPAPER tablet has an 11-inch display and a questionable chip from $229
snippet: TCL has launched a new tablet using its NXTPAPER display tech, with the TCL Tab A1 NXTPAPER now available for a reasonable price, but with a questionable chipset choice. more…
fullText:
TCL has launched a new tablet using its NXTPAPER display tech, with the TCL Tab A1 NXTPAPER now available for a reasonable price, but with a questionable chipset choice.

Expanding on the existing Tab A1 line, TCL’s new 11-inch models offer NXTPAPER and non-NXTPAPER versions that share essentially the same specs and design. The only difference is that the NXTPAPER version has a matte finish to the display while also including a compatible stylus.

The TCL Tab A1 (11-inch) duo offers up an 11-inch, 2112×1320 90Hz display which has a 16:10 aspect ratio. Both tablets run Android 16 out of the box, an 8,000 mAh battery, and 6GB of RAM with 128GB of storage (and a microSD card slot). 

It’s all powered by the MediaTek Helio G100 chipset, a low-cost chip that debuted in 2024 as a very minor upgrade to the Helio G99 that launched back in 2022. It probably makes for a perfectly usable tablet, but it does seem a little underpowered, at least on the NXTPAPER version that sells for as much as $299. You probably won’t see that price often, though, as TCL is selling the Tab A1 NXTPAPER on its own website for $249, and on Amazon for $229. The non-NXTPAPER version can be had for $179 through TCL’s website or on Amazon.

title: Google Wallet for Android adds 11th digital state ID, first addition in 10 months
snippet: After a 10-month pause, Google Wallet is now rolling out support for Ohio state IDs on Android. more…
fullText:
After a 10-month pause, Google Wallet is now rolling out support for Ohio state IDs on Android.

Open the Google Wallet app, tap the ‘plus’ button next to “View more” at the bottom, IDs & personal info, and then Driver’s license or state ID. This reveals Ohio as the 12th Google Wallet option. It joins Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Georgia, Iowa, Maryland, Montana, New Mexico, North Dakota, and Puerto Rico.

The card design shows the Northern Cardinal, which is Ohio’s state bird.

The set-up process requires taking photos of the front and back of your physical card, as well as a short video of your face for verification that gets sent to the OH BMV. This review can take a few minutes with a notification confirming once it’s available. You’ll also get an email confirmation from the state agency.

	

First, tap on the reader or scan your QR code: Your personal info won’t be shared yet. On your phone, review what info you want to share.

Next, review what info will be shared: Make sure you’re comfortable sharing the info they request

You don’t need to hand your phone to anyone: Your ID will be securely shared using Bluetooth, so make sure it’s on

Lastly, verify it’s you to share your info: For extra security, verify that this ID is yours using your face, fingerprint, password, or PIN

“Details” next to “Show code” lets you enable an “Activity history,” while “Driver’s License information” lists license number, date of expiry, address, and more.

IDs can be read via NFC or by having the QR code scanned. It is accepted at some airports by the TSA. Officially, you still have to carry your ID card as the one on your phone “does not replace the requirement for individuals to carry a physical card.” 

Your device must be running Android 8+ and have a screen lock, with Bluetooth and Nearby devices enabled. A state ID can be deleted from Google Wallet any time or remotely via myaccount.google.com. As a private pass, it does not get synced to the cloud and is only available on one device.

Tap Personal Info.

Scroll to “Digital ID.”

Tap Manage Digital ID.

Next to the ID or license that you want to remove, tap Delete.

Confirm that you want to delete your ID from your device and Google Account.

fullText:
9to5Mac is brought to you by Memoket: The Memoket Gem is an 11g AI wearable that slots beside your Apple Watch in a co-wear band. Press once to capture a conversation, and Gem connects it to what you discussed weeks ago — surfacing the earlier thread with a source link. From $179, shipping August 2026.

In 2023, early adopters were just getting to know ChatGPT and AI chatbot tech. Three years later, OpenAI’s Codex agent, now part of the ChatGPT desktop app, has brought about a similar season of learning. Here’s how I’m using ChatGPT, Codex, and more on my Mac.

The summer I turned Codex

Like a billion other people, ChatGPT has become a regular part of my tech stack. But I’m a writer, not a programmer, so Codex as an agentic coding app didn’t immediately appeal to me.

That started to change in April when Codex for Mac added Computer Use.

First, a brief history lesson. 

Back in December 2014, Ari Weinstein and friends launched a new iOS 8 app for mobile automation. Here’s my 9to5Mac coverage of Workflow’s launch, a friendlier version of OS X’s Automator made for iPhone and iPad.

In March 2017, Apple bought Workflow. Workflow gained system integration and became Apple Shortcuts with iOS 12 in 2018.

Weinstein and other Workflow veterans later left Apple to create Software Applications Incorporated. The startup previewed Sky, a modern AI assistant on the Mac, before being acquired by OpenAI.

Sky never publicly launched. Instead, Codex for Mac delivered the technology in April in the form of the Computer Use plugin. 

So excited to share that we're bringing Computer Use to Codex. Computer Use lets Codex see, click, and type into your Mac apps, with its own cursor.

It's a magical feeling to have agents using your apps in the background, and still get to use your computer at the same time. pic.twitter.com/wdgxiHAKyX

— Ari Weinstein (@AriX) April 16, 2026

Trusting an AI with using your Mac, especially in the background, requires a level of trust. I don’t know what my adoption of Codex and Computer Use would be like without the history behind it.

I just know that, for me, there was a great level of inherited trust and continuity that gave me confidence in the system.

Here’s where I admit that Workflow and Shortcuts never super clicked for me. I’ve used both systems with tools that others built, but I haven’t been a builder myself.

Codex has completely changed that, but not overnight.

ChatGPT to Codex to ChatGPT … a journey

I initially found Codex to be too intimidating and outside my comfort zone compared to ChatGPT. Now ChatGPT without Codex feels like a toy. 

I’ve mentioned before that it was actually a toy-like feature inside Codex called Pets that served as the training wheels for me. (The real Codex pets are the personal projects you hatch along the way.)

I started using Codex daily in May. The first project I started with Codex is a Mac app called Flow — because it helps my story writing flow. It’s mostly a way to monitor app releases and updates. 

In my early 9to5Mac days, I used iTunes on the Mac for this purpose. It required local (and otherwise unusable) iPhone app files. More recently, I’ve used iPhone Mirroring to check the App Store on my iPhone for app updates as part of my work routine.

Describing this “workflow” to Codex started the process of building Flow. Being able to describe every little feature and change that I wanted, as if I was messaging a colleague, made it feel natural.

Because it’s my first project and built just for me, the icon is my first initial, handwritten by me (Apple Pencil, iPad Pro, Procreate), made with Apple’s Icon Composer Mac app.

Closing the loop

Because you can iterate forever, I’ve found it’s important to “close the loop” and consider a project mostly complete.

With Flow, I’ve definitely moved to the stage where I can measure the number of my 9to5Mac posts that originate from using the tool. This is an important distinction from measuring the amount of time spent invested into building the tool itself.

But because building with Codex has been such a joy, there are naturally other projects that have followed. You can just make your own Mac apps, specific to your very particular needs.

In my case, I’ve made more modern versions of apps I’ve used for years, tailored to my specific needs, right down to very specific narrow column widths.

This is very specific, but it’s very cool to me. I have a column view for social media, and a column view for RSS, on either side of my Mac display. Both are 275 pixels wide (and made for macOS 27 Golden Gate specifically). This is much narrower than the solutions I previously used, which weren’t even optimized for macOS 26.

Using X2 and Flume, I’m able to open up a significant amount of screen real estate in the middle without overlapping windows.

Social media and RSS are also mostly passive viewing apps for me. By default, toolbar button accent colors turn gray for non-active windows. But because these apps are made for me, I’m able to express that I prefer the touch of color to stay active, just desaturate a step, adding a splash of joy to my Mac.

But wait, there’s more 

At this point, if you’re still reading, this post is probably starting to feel like the guy who just discovered going to the gym and can’t stop telling everyone about how great it makes them feel. 

For that reason, I’ll just flag a few more hobby projects that Codex has unlocked for me.

First, Better Remote. It’s on the Mac App Store. If you’re already using your Mac, it makes tvOS feel like just another Mac app. Here’s a look at the update currently in the queue.

Outside of work (and spending more time outside), iterating on Better Remote has been my main side project this summer. The project started in June.

Second, Better Battery. I adore the look of macOS 27 Golden Gate, but I can’t read the battery indicator with the percentage displayed as well.

Prior to Codex, I’d probably write a blog post as a feature request to flag the issue. Instead, I’ve been able to make my own solution — during the beta period — which others can use for free.

I’ve also been testing ChatGPT Sites with a custom domain to make sharing all of this easier. I initially thought OpenAI’s Sites feature wasn’t really for me.

Publishing Better Remote on the Mac App Store required a web presence, though, which gave me a reason to test the ChatGPT/Codex feature.

Now I’m pretty excited to see where ChatGPT Sites can go from here. OpenAI recently added shared site management tools, and there’s a big opportunity for a more defined interface — like a modern Apple iWeb.

It’s still very early days for these tools, but I find it all very promising and exciting. I haven’t had this much fun using my Mac to make things since GarageBand two decades ago.

Featured image: Fosi Audio MD3 MagSafe DAC, customized with Codex

9to5Mac is brought to you by Memoket:

Every day, important conversations happen in meetings, on calls, over coffee, and on the go. By the time you sit down at your desk, half the details are gone. And AI tools are only as smart as the context you feed them.

Your iPhone stops recording the moment a call comes in. Your Apple Watch can’t capture what’s happening across the table. Neither connects what was said today to a decision made three weeks ago.

Memoket Gem was built for exactly that gap. An 11g AI wearable that captures conversations with one press and connects them across time. When a topic comes up that you discussed weeks ago, Gem surfaces it automatically with a source link. Everything flows directly into ChatGPT, Claude, Slack, and Notion.

For Apple Watch users, Gem slots into a custom co-wear band alongside your Watch on the same wrist. Two devices, completely unobtrusive.

At 0.4 oz with 20 hours of battery and 153 languages supported, Gem disappears into your day while capturing everything that matters.

Early bird pricing from $179 at memoket.ai. Ships August 2026.

title: Here’s everything new in Android 17 QPR2 Beta 4 [Gallery]
snippet: While not as big as the last release, Android 17 QPR2 Beta 4 is a sizable update ahead of the stable December release. more…
fullText:
While not as big as the last release, Android 17 QPR2 Beta 4 is a sizable update ahead of the stable December release.

Over the coming hours, we’ll dive into all of Android 17 QPR2 Beta 4’s new features and every single change. (The newest updates will be at the top of this list. Be sure to check back often and tell us what you find in the comments below.) Android 17 QPR2 Beta 3 screenshots appear on the left and Android 17 QPR2 Beta 4 on the right.

If you want to quickly install Android 17 QPR2 Beta 3 on your compatible Pixel 6a, Pixel 7, Pixel 7 Pro, Pixel 7a, Pixel Tablet, Pixel Fold, Pixel 8, Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel 8a, Pixel 9, Pixel 9 Pro, Pixel 9 Pro XL, Pixel 9 Pro Fold, Pixel 9a, Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro, Pixel 10 Pro XL, Pixel 10 Pro Fold, and Pixel 10a, be sure to check out our step-by-step guide.

Updating…

	

Private Compute Core log

Private Compute Core is a “secure environment that is isolated from the rest of the operating system and apps” that Google first launched in 2021. This on-device processing powers Now Playing, Smart Reply, Live Translate, Live Caption, Google Messages Spam Detection, and Cough & Snore Detection.

Settings > Security & privacy > Privacy dashboard > Data logging

Agents dashboard

Settings > Security & privacy > Privacy controls > Agents

Voice broadcast Quick Settings Tile

Consolidates the AI-powered Notification summaries and organizer, as well as Notification cooldown 

New badges in Wallpaper & style

Status bar customization

Learn more

Pixel 11 support is coming

CP41.260814.003.C2 is for the Pixel 11, 11 Pro, 11 Pro XL, and 11 Pro Fold, but it’s not available yet as of Friday afternoon. Officially, this build “will be available soon.”

Platform stability milestone

Bug fixes

Enabling the “render apps below the cutout area” developer setting caused a transparent status bar on the launcher after exiting fullscreen video playback. (Issue #295747911)

A thermal management issue that caused devices to overheat and unexpectedly reboot during use. (Issue #437116407)

An issue preventing screen mirroring to external USB-C XR glasses. (Issue #439269938)

Gesture navigation became unresponsive when rendering apps below the display cutout. (Issue #441378954)

The 80% battery limit optimization caused excessive charge times during the final 2% threshold. (Issue #477009501, Issue #476803337)

A launcher UI issue where searching for apps in the app drawer failed to process text input. (Issue #505157934, Issue #527921034, Issue #530531588, Issue #537704656)

Invoking the power menu via hardware buttons caused a missing background blur effect behind the navigation bar. (Issue #537202501)

An issue where phone call audio defaulted to the phone speaker instead of connected Bluetooth devices. (Issue #537908014, Issue #541501134, Issue #541772860, Issue #545047074)

A Recents app switcher rendering bug where the first task card could intermittently freeze and visually clip behind other apps during horizontal scrolling. (Issue #530484511, Issue #505564040, Issue #545574713, Issue #551022006)

An audio service resource lock triggered during screen recording that prevented microphone usage across apps and input methods like Gboard and Gemini until a device restart. (Issue #538229807)

A System UI visual inconsistency where turning off the screen from the home screen triggered a plain fade instead of the power-button screen-off animation. (Issue #541261786)

A low-contrast rendering issue in dark mode where the connected Wi-Fi settings cog icon was barely visible. (Issue #536320341)

Enabling 3D mode on connected smart glasses resulted in a blank screen. (Issue #536628506)

A User Interface issue that prevented the notification bar from being pulled all the way down. (Issue #539244095, Issue #547801203, Issue #547017781, Issue #546896889, Issue #547163658, Issue #547281675)

An issue where WebGL applications could freeze or crash the browser process when combining shadow maps with vertex color attributes by resolving an invalid memory read in the PowerVR GPU driver’s texture state processing. (Issue #541322087)

Low-light Face Unlock failures bypassed Fingerprint Unlock and forced PIN entry. (Issue #547597971, Issue #545329611, Issue #541723970)

title: Enhanced geothermal notches another win as Google buys 400 MW from Fervo
snippet: Fervo's deal with Google could expand to 1 gigawatt of geothermal power, enough to supply a very large AI data center in Utah.
fullText:
Geothermal energy company Fervo notched another win as Google agreed to buy nearly half a gigawatt of electricity to power a planned new data center in Utah.

The power purchase agreement, announced Tuesday, commits Google to buying 396 megawatts from Fervo’s Cape Station power plant in Utah, which is expected to come online in 2028. Google has the option through June 2030 to buy an additional 600 megawatts.

The deal arrives as Google and other hyperscalers are scouring the country for new sources of electricity. For years, Google has been one of the larger purchasers of clean energy in the U.S. and elsewhere, buying electricity from wind, solar, and batteries to make good on its promise to reach net-zero emissions by 2030.

But in April, that goal became harder to reach after Google inked a deal with data center developer Crusoe for 933 megawatts of natural gas power in Texas.

The Fervo deal could help Google fuel its AI ambitions without significantly imperiling its net-zero goal.

Fervo is permitted to develop up to 2 gigawatts of geothermal energy at Cape Station, but Sarah Jewett, Fervo’s senior vice president of strategy, told TechCrunch in May that a third-party engineer said the site holds enough heat to generate twice as much electricity. 

If fully developed, those 4 gigawatts would about double the entire geothermal generating capacity in the U.S., according to a recent U.S. Department of Energy report. It’s possible that Google’s gigawatt deal could grow even larger if Fervo’s operations go as planned.

Enhanced geothermal technologies, like the kind Fervo has developed, can tap deeper sources of heat. Using those technologies, the U.S. could generate up to 57 terawatts of electricity, according to the report.

Fervo and Google’s new deal adds to the pair’s long-standing relationship. The companies have been working together for more than five years, with Google buying some of Fervo’s first electrons. Recently, Google invested in Fervo’s last funding round before the geothermal startup went public.

Though Fervo’s stock popped on its first day of trading, it shed those gains and more over the last few months. News of the Google deal, though, drove the stock up about 30% yesterday before traders took some profits today.

Tim De Chant is a senior climate reporter at TechCrunch. He has written for a wide range of publications, including Wired magazine, the Chicago Tribune, Ars Technica, The Wire China, and NOVA Next, where he was founding editor. 

De Chant is also a lecturer in MIT’s Graduate Program in Science Writing, and he was awarded a Knight Science Journalism Fellowship at MIT in 2018, during which time he studied climate technologies and explored new business models for journalism. He received his PhD in environmental science, policy, and management from the University of California, Berkeley, and his BA degree in environmental studies, English, and biology from St. Olaf College.

title: The Builders Stage brings practical strategies for scaling startups to TechCrunch Disrupt 2026
snippet: The Builders Stage is returning to TechCrunch Disrupt, bringing together founders, startup operators, and investors for practical conversations on what it takes to build and scale.
fullText:
The Builders Stage is returning to TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, bringing together founders, startup operators, and investors for practical conversations on what it takes to build and scale successful companies.

Hear from startup and venture leaders shaping the tech ecosystem, including Grant Lee, CEO and co-founder of Gamma; Leah Solivan, founder and general partner at Precedent.vc; Robby Stein, VP of Product at Google; and more. Through candid conversations and real-world case studies, speakers will share actionable insights on fundraising, hiring, go-to-market strategy, AI, and the operational decisions that fuel startup growth.

Join more than 10,000 founders, investors, startup operators, and technology leaders at Moscone Center in San Francisco on October 13-15. Register today and save before our next ticket price increase.

Image Credits:TechCrunch

Built for founders who are ready to scale

Building a startup is one thing. Building a company that can scale is another challenge entirely. The Builders Stage is one of six industry-focused stages at Disrupt 2026, dedicated to helping founders navigate the challenges of growth, from raising capital and hiring top talent to building go-to-market engines and preparing for the jump from seed to Series A.

Every session delivers practical strategies you can put to work immediately, plus opportunities to engage directly with speakers during live Q&A. Secure your pass to Disrupt 2026 today and save up to $330 before rates increase.

Image Credits:Slava Blazer Photography / Flickr (opens in a new window)

Without further ado, here’s your first look at the Builders Stage agenda, with more speakers and sessions to be announced as we get closer to the event.

Builders Stage agenda

How to Win When You’re Not Building AI

With Shan Shan, Investment Manager, Baillie Gifford; and Yuri Sagalov, Managing Director at General Catalyst

AI may dominate the world of venture, but many enduring companies won’t be those that sell AI models or agents. This session is for founders competing for attention in an AI-obsessed market. Panelists break down what actually matters now: efficient growth, retention, revenue quality, and disciplined execution, and why fundamentals, not hype, still build breakout businesses.

What Happens When OpenAI Ships Your Roadmap

With Michel Tricot, CEO and Co-founder, Airbyte; Rob Toews, Partner, Radical Ventures; and Linda Tong, CEO, Webflow

Nearly all AI founders have the same worry these days: What if OpenAI or Anthropic launches a product that competes with mine? Even strong products are at risk of becoming features of the larger players. This session explores where defensibility exists and what founders can do if they do face competition from rapidly evolving AI giants.

Building the Next Generation of AI Giants

With Jas Khaira, Global Head, Blackstone N1

AI startups are scaling faster, and demanding more capital, than any generation before them. Jas Khaira, Global Head of Blackstone N1, shares what separates enduring companies from early momentum, how founders should think about capital as they scale, and what Blackstone looks for when backing the next generation of category-defining businesses.

Competing for AI Talent: Pay, Equity, and Retention

With Matt Birnbaum, Founder, Wylder.co, Ioana Hreninciuc, Runware, Atli Thorkelsson, VP, Talent Network, Redpoint Ventures

The growth of AI startups has made hiring and retention more difficult for every tech company. From competing for AI talent to navigating secondary sales, founders are rethinking the human infrastructure of their startups. As incentives and employee expectations rapidly evolve, this session explores how companies are adapting compensation, culture, and team-building strategies to attract and retain top talent in a fundamentally changed market.

Winning Pre-Seed Without a Product

With Puneet Agarwal, Managing Partner, True Ventures; Austin Clements, Managing Partner, Slauson and Co; and Sandhya Venkatachalam, Founder and Managing Partner, Axiom Partners

Founders are increasingly expected to compete for capital before they even have a product. At the pre-seed stage, investors are betting on story, conviction, and founder-market fit. This session breaks down how to build credibility before revenue exists so investors will cut that first check.

From MVP to Billions of Users: How Product Decisions Must Change at Scale

With Robby Stein, VP, Product, Google

The instincts that win when building your first minimum viable product can break you at a billion-user scale. In this fireside, Robby Stein shares how product decision-making changes when every update impacts billions of users. Hear how teams balance speed with trust and innovation with reliability at one of the world’s largest product organizations.

Hiring When AI Is a Co-Founder

With Josh Reeves, CEO and Co-founder, Gusto; more speakers to be announced

Early-stage companies are no longer just building with AI; they’re hiring it. As AI agents take on engineering, support, and operations, the definition of an early team is being rewritten. This session explores how founders decide what humans should own versus what gets delegated to AI, and how high-growth startups are building hybrid teams without losing speed, accountability, or culture.

Rebuilding Consumer Products for the AI Era

With Maria Angelidou-Smith, CPO, Reddit

AI isn’t just adding features, it’s forcing product teams to rethink how people search, discover, communicate, travel, and make decisions. Leaders from Reddit, Square and Uber discuss how they’re redesigning products used by millions, what users actually want from AI, and where product leaders should resist the temptation to automate everything.

M&A Is Now an Early-Stage Strategy

With Karl Alomar, Managing Partner, M13 and Lindsey Mignano, Founder, Mignano Law Group

The smartest founders today aren’t just building for IPOs; they’re also building with possible acquisitions in mind from day one. As exits shift and capital tightens, understanding M&A early has become a competitive advantage. This session breaks down how founders can create the possibility of such an option through product strategy and partnerships. It delves into how big-dollar startup outcomes actually happen, even for small companies.

The Series A in 2027

Jahanvi Sardana, Partner, Index Ventures; Shailendra Singh, Managing Director, Peak XV; and Janelle Teng Wade, Partner, Bessemer Venture Partners

Series A is getting harder, with VCs growing more demanding. For founders planning to raise in the next one to two years, this session breaks down what “fundable” will actually mean in 2027. Hear how top investors are redefining the metrics, teams, and traction that matter now, what outdated fundraising playbooks no longer work, and how companies can separate from the pack in the next funding cycle.

The 90-Day GTM: Why $0–$10M ARR Is the New Baseline (and How to Actually Get There)

With Ryan Meadows, Chief Revenue Officer, Lovable; and Tomasz Tunguz, General Partner and Founder, Theory Ventures; Ben Broca, Founder, Polsia

The definition of traction has changed. What once took years is now expected in months, and $0 to $10 million ARR is increasingly becoming the new early-stage baseline. This session breaks down how AI-enabled execution, faster distribution, and shifting investor expectations are compressing GTM timelines, and the tactical levers founders need in the first 90 days to accelerate revenue and stand out fast.

The Real Tokenmaxxing: How the Best AI Companies Navigate a Multi-Model World

With Mo Jomaa, Partner, Capital G; and Zuzanna Stamirowska, CEO and Co-founder, Pathway; more speakers to be announced

The frontier is moving faster than any single model can keep up with, and the teams building the most successful AI products are increasingly orchestrating across many models rather than betting on just one. This panel brings together founders and operators at the center of that shift to discuss how they evaluate new models, manage cost and reliability at scale, and architect products that can evolve as quickly as the underlying technology.

Revealing AI Disruptors 60: What Can AI Do Next?

With Shay Grinfield, Greenfield Partners

The AI conversation is shifting from what models can say to what they can actually do. Agents are navigating the open web and completing work, AI systems are taking on increasingly ambitious research, intelligent machines are beginning to operate beyond the screen, and a new infrastructure layer is emerging to make all of this possible at scale. 

Greenfield Partners’ Shay Grinfeld sits down with founders building across these emerging areas to separate what’s real today from what’s coming next, and explore where the biggest new opportunities are taking shape. The conversation will culminate in the reveal of Greenfield Partners’ 2026 AI Disruptors 60, spotlighting the companies Greenfield and TechCrunch believe are pushing AI into new territory.

PMF Red Flags: How to Tell If You Really Have It

With Rajeev Dham, Managing Director, Sapphire Ventures; and Rahul Vohra, Founder and Head of Superhuman Mail; more speakers to be announced

In an AI hype cycle, product-market fit signals are easier to fake and harder to trust. Founders are mistaking early excitement, usage spikes, and pilot wins for durable traction. This session breaks down what false PMF actually looks like, how investors and operators separate real retention from hype-driven adoption, and the signals that indicate whether a company has true pull or just temporary momentum.

The Zero-to-1K Playbook: How to Get Your First 1,000 Customers Without a Marketing Budget

With Grant Lee, CEO and Co-founder, Gamma; Leah Solivan, Founder and General Partner, Precedent.vc; and Elia Wallen, Founder and CEO, Engine

Early customer acquisition is not about marketing spend; it’s about founder-led distribution and relentless execution. Most startups at zero to one do not have budget, brand, or scale, only urgency and creativity. This session breaks down how founders are landing their first customers through community building, product-led growth, founder-led sales, strategic outbound, and word-of-mouth momentum.

Yes, It’s Hard to Be a Founder: An Honest Conversation

With Nell Daly, Co-founder and Managing Partner, Revenge Capital; David H. Rosmarin, Associate Professor, Harvard Medical School; and Jack Withinshaw, Co-founder and Chief Commercial Officer, Airspeeder

Company building is as psychologically demanding as it is strategic, and most founder narratives understate that reality. In this candid conversation, founders and mental performance experts unpack the hidden costs of high-growth environments, from burnout and decision fatigue to the identity strain of sustained pressure, and share the systems, habits, and mental frameworks that help leaders endure and perform at a high level.

So You’ve Got a Hit Product. How Does Your Company Do It Again?

With Filip Kaliszan, CEO and Co-founder, Verkada; and Aaron Jacobson, Partner, New Enterprise Associates; Maddi Holman, General Partner, Daring Ventures 

Most startups stall out because they build a single great product instead of a repeatable multi-product engine. Join a venture capitalist and two founders as they reveal the precise operational playbook for capital allocation, systemizing internal innovation, and engineering a compounding “Second Act” before the core product’s growth curve flattens.

Hiring, Compensation and Culture in the Most Competitive Market Ever

With Matt Birnbaum, Founder, Wylder.co; and Atli Thorkelsson, VP, Talent Network, Redpoint Ventures; more speakers to be announced

No question about it, the growth of AI startups has made hiring and retention for all tech companies more difficult. From competing for AI talent to secondary sales, founders are rethinking the human infrastructure of their startups. As hiring, incentives, and employee expectations rapidly evolve, this session explores how companies are adapting compensation, culture, and team-building strategies to attract and retain top talent in a fundamentally changed startup environment.

How to Create Viral Growth and Capitalize on It

With Zach Yadegari, Founder, Cal AI

Startups can go from zero to viral overnight, but sustaining that momentum is a completely different challenge. In this fireside, Zach Yadegari shares how Cal AI navigated rapid growth, product pressure, and the realities of building in a distribution-driven market. Hear the lessons behind turning breakout attention into durable retention and long-term company building.

The High-Conviction Filter: What We Learned From the Battlefield

With Alexa von Tobel, Inspired Capital; and Chi-Hua Chien, Co-founder and Managing Partner, Goodwater Capital; more speakers to be announced

What separates the breakout companies from the rest at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026? In this candid debrief, Startup Battlefield judges unpack the trends and founder qualities that stood out in real time, from shifting investor expectations to the narratives that resonated most this year. The conversation will also explore how startup storytelling is evolving and what happens after the spotlight, including the realities of maintaining momentum and surviving the critical 12 months after a major launch, funding round, or Startup Battlefield appearance.

Ask the Investors

With Stacy Brown-Philpot, Founder & Managing Partner at Cherryrock Capital; Chi-Hua Chien, Co-founder & Managing Partner, Goodwater Capital; Dayna Grayson, Construct Capital; Carter Reum, Co-founder and Managing Partner, M13; Alexa Von Tobel, Inspired Capital

What makes an investor say yes? In this audience-led Q&A, the Startup Battlefield finals judges take your toughest questions on what separates a fundable startup from the rest: team, traction, market opportunity, pitch delivery, red flags, and more. Come ready to ask and get candid answers straight from the investors making the decisions.

Join the conversations and make the connections at Disrupt

If you’re ready to build smarter, scale faster, and learn from the leaders shaping the future of startups, secure your pass to TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 today.

title: Apple paying 400% more for iPhone 18 Pro memory, says TrendForce
snippet: A new market intelligence report suggests that Apple will be paying four times more for iPhone 18 Pro memory than it did for last year’s model. TrendForce says that Apple won’t be passing on the full impact to customers, and will be increasingly looking to Services revenue to offset higher hardware manufacturing costs … more…
fullText:
A new market intelligence report suggests that Apple will be paying four times more for iPhone 18 Pro memory than it did for last year’s model.

TrendForce says that Apple won’t be passing on the full impact to customers, and will be increasingly looking to Services revenue to offset higher hardware manufacturing costs … 

Apple announced significant price increases across most of its products back in June, stating that it had done everything possible to delay this but no longer had any choice.

The company did not raise the prices of its existing iPhones at the time, but that’s expected to change next week. TrendForce pointed to dramatically increased memory costs for the new models.

For the 256GB Pro model, memory costs in 3Q26 are expected to be nearly 400% higher than a year earlier. Despite Apple’s efforts to negotiate lower prices for other components, these savings are unlikely to offset the resulting pressure on overall BOM costs. An increase in retail prices appears increasingly unavoidable while hardware costs remain elevated. 

Apple is not expected to pass on the full increase in memory costs in iPhone pricing. Current expectations are for an increase of around $100 over the iPhone 17 Pro. 

That’s because substantial price increases lead to even the biggest Apple fans upgrading their products less frequently. TrendForce says Apple will not want to sacrifice continued growth, also pointing to a weak macroeconomic environment leading to more cautious consumer spending.

The company predicts that the iPhone Ultra, Apple’s first folding model, could start at anything up to $2,299 with the top-end configuration exceeding $3,000.

title: Plaud’s new AI recorder is a pair of earbuds
snippet: Plaud got its jumpstart in popularity with a view on agentic AI that centered around recording summaries for students and professionals. Now, it wants to become a full-time assistant with the Plaud One earbuds. more…
fullText:
Plaud got its jumpstart in popularity with a view on agentic AI that centered around recording summaries for students and professionals. Now, it wants to become a full-time assistant with the Plaud One earbuds.

You might be familiar with the Plaud Note Pro, and that might be just because it looks like a modern retro voice recorder. It essentially is – recorded audio gets turned into highly detailed AI summaries through the Plaud app. Over the last year or so, Plaud has implemented more features to position the app as not just a summary tool, but an assistant of sorts.

The Plaud One is the next step, starting at $249. Unlike the Note Pro, the Plaud One Explorer Edition looks and acts like a pair of earbuds. The case has a lot of the same new-age retro design cues as the Note voice recorders, and it doubles as its own sort of recorder when the earbuds aren’t in use.

It isn’t an always-listening device, but it seems to skirt the line before it becomes invasive. Plaud says users can record everything the Note can, but the earbuds can also capture online meetings. It sounds like the Plaud One earbuds can capture the audio it plays, which could circumvent the difficulty of recording a call with a third-party device.

	

The earbuds themselves have all of the expected features, like ANC and transparency mode. Plaud notes they are equipped with 12mm dynamic drivers and support LDAC audio, surprisingly. With the charging case, the battery life is stated at 36 hours. On a single charge, the earbuds can record or play audio for up to 6 hours (without ANC). The case, however, can record for up to 25 hours continuously on a charge with 21 days of standby power on the 830mAh battery.

The big thing here seems to be Plaud Agent, which runs on Plaud Intelligence. In all respects, it’s an AI agent that handles tasks using the context surrounding your recorded meetings and conversations. Plaud says the Plaud One will integrate with apps like Gmail, Google Calendar, Notion, and Slack to perform tasks. Just like another agentic AI platform, the user has the option to manage skills so it does the job right.

The Plaud One earbuds seem like a logical evolution of the Note Pro and the app itself. How it handles summaries has always been extremely helpful in my personal usage, but it can be pricey.

It sounds like Plaud One will use usage credits the same way the Note recorder does. It’s unclear whether Plaud Agent usage counts towards those credits, or if, like the previous recorders, generating summaries on recorded material is what drains your limits.

The Plaud One Explorer Edition earbuds are available for pre-order starting today. Shipments will begin in Q4 2026.

title: Here’s the likely reason the iPhone Ultra isn’t getting an Apple Pencil
snippet: A report yesterday suggested that Apple considered making a special version of the Apple Pencil for the upcoming iPhone Ultra before deciding against it. Bloomberg suggests that there are three reasons behind this decision, one of them being a desire not to conflict with the position adopted by Steve Jobs when launching the original iPhone. However, this was almost certainly not the deciding factor … more…
fullText:
A report yesterday suggested that Apple considered making a special version of the Apple Pencil for the upcoming iPhone Ultra before deciding against it.

Bloomberg suggests that there are three reasons behind this decision, one of them being a desire not to conflict with the position adopted by Steve Jobs when launching the original iPhone. However, this was almost certainly not the deciding factor …

The idea of a shorter Apple Pencil that could be used with the iPhone Ultra is certainly an appealing idea on the face of it. The device is essentially an iPhone that turns into an iPad mini, so giving it some of the same capabilities obviously makes a lot of sense. 

Samsung gave its Galaxy Note phablets an S-Pen stylus when the device was launched back in 2011. The thinking was that this was a device that would in part substitute for a paper notebook, and it survived for a decade with a definite fanbase before being discontinued in 2021.

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman lists three reasons Apple decided against the idea in the end:

It would have made the device awkward to hold, with a Pencil on the side rather than the top

It would have conflicted with Steve’s view of a stylus being a poor substitute for a finger

It would have made unsightly marks on the display

I’m not convinced the first of these would have been a major consideration, as mounting it to the top of the device would have been an option. Although this would have required a very short design, it would still have worked well enough, I think.

I’m also not persuaded by the second. Steve’s objection was not to the fact that you could use a stylus with a smartphone, but rather that existing models required this. Designing the iPhone so that it was practical to use with a finger was the breakthrough.

In any case, Steve also famously rejected touchscreens on Macs because he felt the ergonomics were terrible, but we’re still expecting the upcoming MacBook Pro model to incorporate one, so clearly Apple isn’t afraid to contradict the positions once taken by its co-founder.

I think the third factor was the one that actually killed the idea. A folding display necessarily has a far thinner and softer surface than those of existing devices. Apple reportedly waited a long time to launch the first folding iPhone precisely because it was concerned about both the appearance and longevity of the display, and allowing an Apple Pencil to be repeatedly scraped across it would have put both at risk.

If Apple can ever solve this problem, would you want to see an Apple Pencil Mini for use with a future iPhone Ultra? Please let us know in the comments.

title: Anthropic’s Content Checker Tool Is Here, With One Big Catch
snippet: You can look for Claude’s watermarks in a lot of files, but not in text just yet.
fullText:
Just a couple of weeks after Anthropic announced it would roll out digital watermarks for text generated with its Claude AI tools, the company has introduced a page where you can check files to see if Claude helped make them.

The page, at claude.com/check-content, lets you upload files with a quick spot check and will confirm, “This file shows signs it was processed by Claude,” if it finds content credentials embedded in the file.

But if you’re hoping to prove that someone used Claude for a term paper or want to see if someone’s texts weren’t actually written by the human you’re talking to, you’re going to need to wait. The checker currently works with only a limited number of file types, and none of them are text formats. Instead, the checker accepts multimedia files, including JPEGs, GIFs, MP3s and MOVs — basically image, audio or video files.

A spokesperson for Anthropic told CNET that the tool is specifically to check for Claude’s use through an industry standard called C2PA; a broader AI detection tool is in the works, but not yet available.

“Text checking is via our Detection API (separate tool) and in private preview, and we hope to share more about it in the months ahead,” the spokesperson said. This aligns with a note on the check content tool reads, “To detect watermarks embedded in text we have a Detection API which is currently in private preview to eligible organizations as required under EU law.”

Anthropic has said that its watermarking of text that Claude produces won’t affect the quality, speed or cost of outputs and that these watermarks won’t be visible or affect how text functions or appears. But they will remain with text from Claude even if it’s copied and pasted from one place to another. Anthropic has a sign-up form for businesses or organizations that want to be added to the list for access to the watermark detector.

Anthropic said in its email to CNET that if the C2PA standard expands to include additional file formats, its checker tool will likely adopt them as well.

How does Anthropic’s new checker work?

The free web-based tool has a drag-and-drop option, or you can click to add a file from your device or Google Drive on mobile. According to the website, the file you choose stays on your device or file service, and the checker only reads the file’s credentials, not the file itself.

“Your file is never stored or used for any other purpose,” the page says.

In CNET’s testing of the tool, the detector correctly flagged an image file that was converted in Claude from a PowerPoint presentation. For files that the detector said were not shown to be processed by Claude, a message is shown that reads, “We couldn’t find any signs that this file was processed by Claude. That doesn’t rule it out. Signals like this can be removed when a file is edited, converted, or compressed.”

title: Ford explains why it chose Apple Maps over Google for its new EVs
snippet: Earlier this year, Apple announced a partnership with Ford to bring native Apple Maps integration to the automaker’s upcoming Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) Platform, including what we now know is called the Fathom. more…
fullText:
Earlier this year, Apple announced a partnership with Ford to bring native Apple Maps integration to the automaker’s upcoming Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) Platform, including what we now know is called the Fathom.

In a new interview, Alan Clarke, Ford’s vice president of advanced vehicle projects, elaborated on the decision to use Apple Maps instead of Google Maps and what this means for CarPlay Ultra.

In an interview with GreenCars, Clarke said Ford spoke with Apple, Google, and others about mapping for the Fathom. Ultimately, the company turned to Apple:

“We had to optimize for performance capabilities cost, quality, you name it. We spent time determining which was the best solution.

A couple of things about Apple Maps.

One is that it has gotten so much better over the last few years. It’s a really great solution. The team that we worked with at Apple was very flexible to ensure that we get the absolute best customer experience.”

Clarke said Ford wanted a close working relationship with the Apple Maps team. There are a lot of factors that go into mapping for an EV, including things like range, charger availability, weather, and more. Taking all of those things into account, Ford determined Apple offers “the best solution.” 

“We wanted to make sure that we had really tight integration with that team when we’re talking about the things that have to happen on a vehicle: range estimation and determining how much range you have and how you want to precondition the batteries and how you charge.

You need a great maps provider that has the capability to get elevation, weather, and the maps data to have accurate updated information about chargers.

I think we thought that Apple was the best solution for this vehicle in order to get the customer the best solution.

It’s amazing to be first as well. Apple Maps looks beautiful, and having a large display to be able to put it on we think will be a really big wow factor for our customers when they get to see it.”

Clarke also confirmed that this is Ford integrating Apple Maps into its native, in-car software platform. The automaker is not adopting CarPlay Ultra in the Fathom. Instead, it will offer native Apple Maps, plus standard CarPlay and Android Auto.

With CarPlay support, Ford drivers can choose between Apple Maps, Google Maps, Waze, and other mapping solutions. They can also easily access many excellent third-party CarPlay apps.

You can watch the full interview on the GreenCars YouTube channel.

title: Xiaomi’s Passport Foldable Phone Takes Aim at Apple and Samsung
snippet: Xiaomi has big plans for its push into Europe.
fullText:
I love Xiaomi’s phones and gave the recent Leitzphone — made in collaboration with photography icon Leica — an Editors’ Choice award. But the company has fingers in pies far beyond mobile phones; You’ll find the Xiaomi name on everything from cars, fans, air fryers and robot vacuums, and the company has a trio of home tech products it’s launching at this year’s IFA tech show in Berlin, along with a new passport-shaped foldable set to do battle with Apple’s rumored upcoming folding iPhone.

Leading the company’s home tech lineup is the Mijia Refrigerator Pro Cryo Fresh. The company says this double-door fridge uses tech, including air circulation and nano blue light sterilization, to help keep your food fresher for longer. A weapon against food waste? Quite possibly, but I’ll just be happy if it means I can keep my bell peppers from going all squishy after just a few days. 

Why three drums? Honestly, I’ve no idea.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Then we have the Mijia Tri-Drum Washer Dryer Pro, which uses three separate drums for your clothes washing, with a promised 35% increase in energy efficiency. And finally there’s the Mijia Conditioner Turbo Pro, which boasts huge power for both cooling and heating a room. 

The common thread here? The Mijia brand name. While some of Xiaomi’s smart home products have already been available to buy across Europe, the company is using IFA to bring its wider Mijia brand to Europe. 

“This year’s IFA marks a significant milestone in Xiaomi’s global journey,” said Xu Fei, Xiaomi’s chief marketing officer, in a press release. “This goes beyond bringing more products to Europe. It is about bringing Xiaomi’s technology and ecosystem capabilities to more users across the region.”

Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The company has already announced its plans to bring its range of electric cars — including the SU7, first shown off at MWC 2025 — to Europe starting in 2027. 

Xiaomi also used IFA to show off its upcoming new foldable in the flesh (well, behind glass) for the first time. The Xiaomi 18 Fold will be the first to use the company’s own in-house Xring 03 processor. The phone has been heavily teased already, but seeing it in person I was struck by its similar dimensions to Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 and what we expect to see from Apple’s folding iPhone Ultra in September. Not that that’s a bad thing — this wider format is clearly the way the foldable industry is moving. I appreciate the resulting wider inner display, which is better for watching videos. I’m yet to get my hands on Xiaomi’s new phone but I’m looking forward to trying it out.

Broader specs aren’t yet known — nor are prices or regional availability — but it’s an interesting move to see the company build its own processor rather than rely on Qualcomm’s chips as it has on previous phones, including the Leitzphone. Both Apple and Google have opted to cook up their own processors for their phones and Xiaomi clearly agrees that this is the better long-term strategy when it comes to building a wider ecosystem.

We don’t know the core specs yet, but we do know it’ll run Xiaomi’s own processor.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The phone is due in September and we expect to hear more over the coming days. Final pricing and availability for Xiaomi’s other new smart home products are yet to be announced.

title: Miele Put a Camera in Its New Dishwasher. Here’s Why
snippet: Miele just launched the world’s first dishwasher with built-in camera. Here’s what it does.
fullText:
AI-powered cameras have made their way into most major kitchen appliances. Ovens now watch food as it cooks and tell you when it’s done. Smart refrigerators will ping you when you’re running low on milk or suggest recipes based on what they see lingering in the crisper drawer.

The dishwasher seemed like the final frontier for cameras in kitchen appliances. When I heard that Miele had snuck one into its latest model, unveiled this week at IFA Berlin, I was suspicious. But after a rep walked me through the shiny new Diamond G8 and its camera-centric features, I started to see the appeal.

A camera in Miele’s new dishwasher helps it pick the perfect cycle.

The small camera, fixed to the back of the dishwasher door, gets a clear shot of the dishwasher’s interior. It uses that view to take inventory of what’s inside, recognizing dozens of common kitchen items and tailoring the wash cycle and detergent volume accordingly.

The Diamond G8 is one of the smartest dishwashers we’ve encountered, and it’s easy on the eyes.

Got portable bottles or reusable straws in the dedicated slots? The dishwasher’s brain will recognize them and make sure those items get the spritz they need. Load it up with pots and pans and the camera identifies them, triggering a more intensive cycle so everything comes out clean. A smaller load prompts a lighter cycle, so you’re not wasting more hot water or soap than is needed.

The G8 recognizes straws, flatware, silverware and cookware and adjusts its cycle for optimized cleaning.

The camera also determines how full the dishwasher is. Command the G8 to start when it reaches, say, 80% capacity, and it’ll monitor the load and automatically begin a cycle once it hits that threshold. 

One of my favorite features has nothing to do with the camera

The G8 Diamond takes advantage of fluctuations in electricity prices throughout the day. Tell it to run when electricity is cheapest, and the dishwasher waits for those lower-cost hours before starting its cycle. It’s a small detail, but it points to where Miele – and kitchen appliances more broadly – seem to be headed: machines that don’t just perform a task, but figure out the best and most efficient way to do it.

The dishwasher can be programmed to run when energy costs are cheapest in your area.

Miele’s newly unveiled machine has other AI-powered features that encourage efficiency and performance.  The G8 features careful water and energy monitoring, trackable through Miele’s app. There’s also a smart detergent-dispensing system, first introduced by the brand in 2018, and a beefed-up hot-air drying system, which Miele says gets dishes bone-dry every time.

The camera paired with a smart detergent dispenser doles out just the right amount of soap. 

The Diamond G8 is scheduled to roll out later this year, according to a spokesperson. A retail price is still under wraps, but I expect it to land in the super-premium zone. For a top-performing dishwasher you can buy today, see our list of the best models in 2026.

title: Samsung Galaxy flagships are a hit in the midst of RAMageddon – why?
snippet: As the impact of RAMageddon continues, a couple of this week’s key stories have had me thinking – is the somewhat-boring nature of Samsung’s year-over-year Galaxy flagship refreshes the exact thing making these devices a hit? This issue of 9to5Google Weekender is a part of our newsletter that highlights the biggest Google stories with added commentary and more. fullText:
As the impact of RAMageddon continues, a couple of this week’s key stories have had me thinking – is the somewhat-boring nature of Samsung’s year-over-year Galaxy flagship refreshes the exact thing making these devices a hit?

This issue of 9to5Google Weekender is a part of our newsletter that highlights the biggest Google stories with added commentary and more. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every weekend, and catch our weekday roundups too!

Outside of the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s wider new form factor, 2026 has been a pretty boring year for Samsung Galaxy devices. The Galaxy S26 series is nothing more than a chipset refresh and the Ultra’s Privacy Display, while the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and Flip 8 were both refinements, the latter feeling like it’s on its last legs. Then the Galaxy S26 FE launched this week, which might as well be a poster child (right next to the Pixel 11 series) for the impacts of RAMageddon with its barely-updated package that costs more than last year.

Yet, it’s working.

	

The Galaxy S26 Ultra is, as of the latest update, the world’s most popular Android phone. A $1,300 flagship is outselling Samsung’s uber-cheap budget phones that the company’s success is built on. That’s wild, and it’s also the first time that’s ever happened. It comes alongside foldables as a whole being the one segment of the smartphone market that isn’t shrinking back right now – it’s actually growing steadily. New forecasts from the IDC this week claim that the “cheap smartphone era is over” and that price hikes are essentially never going away, and it’s just looking so bleak.

So how is Samsung actually pulling it off?

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is a hit, and that’s probably in large part because not only is it new, but it directly addresses feedback from users. Thin and light, media-centric designs have been among the biggest requests from foldables right up there alongside ditching the crease – which the Fold 8 also more or less does. The Galaxy S26 Ultra manages this in far less exciting fashion. There was nothing especially new or groundbreaking about the latest Samsung flagship – Privacy Display rules, but it’s not exactly a game-changer – but it proved incredibly popular. I suspect that comes down largely to the simple fact that, if you’re looking for a new smartphone, the Galaxy S26 Ultra is an incredibly safe bet. For the millions on older Galaxy flagships, it’s a no-brainer, especially with trade-in deals thrown up on top.

The strategy is working. No one has to like it, but it is working. On that note, the other thing on my mind was an opinion post asking if Samsung is actually the problem, or if slab smartphone design as a whole has “peaked.” On the one hand, yes, smartphone design has pretty much peaked. On the other, yes, Samsung is the problem. As we’ve discussed repeatedly at this point, Samsung’s existing Galaxy design is an actual problem for users and for the future of smartphone accessories. The market is moving in a direction that Samsung’s phones are incompatible with, and Samsung’s answer to that is apparently to make changes on its highest-end designs and leave the base models stubbornly in the same place. Yes, Samsung is the problem.

But as RAMageddon continues and Samsung’s devices remain a steady rock in the turbulent market, I can’t blame anyone for going for a Galaxy flagship. Boring or not, it checks all of the boxes, and that’s really all that matters for the time being.

title: WhatsApp for Android loophole lets private photos be accessed without unlocking
snippet: A loophole in WhatsApp for Android lets someone see private photos on your device without the device being unlocked, which obviously isn’t supposed to happen. more…
fullText:
A loophole in WhatsApp for Android lets someone see private photos on your device without the device being unlocked, which obviously isn’t supposed to happen. 

First spotted by @VBarraquito on Twitter/X and further confirmed by “Mobile Hacker” and NotebookCheck, a very straightforward flaw exists within WhatsApp for Android that allows someone to access a user’s private photos before the device is unlocked. 

This works by first having a WhatsApp call pop up and be answered – this doesn’t require the phone to be unlocked, just like a standard phone call – at which point the user can tap a button to use filters and effects on their video feed, including Meta’s AI to edit a photo – you can see where this is going. Instead of preventing access to photos, the preview is shown clearly before the phone ever asks to be unlocked with a PIN or biometrics.

This isn’t universal, though. NotebookCheck found that a Galaxy device does force the lockscreen to be unlocked before reaching this step, while Pixel and Oppo devices both allowed the full bypass. The loophole doesn’t exist on iPhone, where WhatsApp is forced to use the native iOS calling UI.

	

The plastic piece here has nothing to do with the exploit, and is presumably only for covering a contact name

The good news: this doesn’t seem to bypass the lockscreen fully, as accessing any other part of the device is still blocked. There’s also not much that can be done with the photos beyond physically seeing them – though a malicious party could use this to take photos of those images with a second device. 

WhatsApp should be able to patch this with an update, but no such update has been announced at this time. The loophole has been reported to both WhatsApp and Google. 

In the meantime, a temporary workaround is to set WhatsApp’s photo/video access to “limited” in Android’s permissions, which breaks the loophole.

title: Philips Hue adds HDMI-free Sync and new 4K Box, Nanoleaf integration, and more app upgrades
snippet: To kick off IFA 2026, Philips Hue announced a new set of sync boxes for its Play lighting. The company also teased a few new app long-awaited changes to the app, and a Nanoleaf partnership that makes your light-up triangles compatible with Philips Hue’s products. more…
fullText:
To kick off IFA 2026, Philips Hue announced a new set of sync boxes for its Play lighting. The company also teased a few new app long-awaited changes to the app, and a Nanoleaf partnership that makes your light-up triangles compatible with Philips Hue’s products.

Philips Hue’s Play Sync Box 8K is an incredible addition to any home theater or living room, but it’s expensive. At around $385, you can connect your TV’s visuals with compatible Philips Hue lights, but that isn’t a feasible option for a lot of users.

Camera-based light kits have become popular for users who want the experience without spending the money on Philips’ good-but-pricey hardware. Options from companies like Govee fill that gap for much less.

Today, though, Philips Hue announced that it’s going to offer a couple of more affordable options for users, starting with its own camera-based sync box. The Philips Hue Play Screen Sync is made up of a single fisheye camera that sits on the top of your TV. It captures colors displayed by your TV, so not only is it more affordable, but it’s input-agnostic. Unlike the 8K Sync Box, this model will work with native TV apps because it isn’t pulling from select HDMI feeds.

	

The Philips Hue Play HDMI Sync Box 4K sits in the middle of three, with a similar experience and compatibility to the higher resolution version. It only has one HDMI connection, which might make it ideal for those that just need a connection to an AVR, instead of media players and consoles.

Both new models can also opt to sync to devices through Bluetooth instead of using a Hue Bridge. That makes the setup simpler. The Hue Bridge and Hue Bridge Pro allow connections to expand to 10 lights, as opposed to a single light strip.

With that, new gradient strip lights were announced for entertainment spaces. Philips Hue says these strips will be available for TVs up to 100 inches.

The IFA announcement continues with an announcement regarding a new partnership with Nanoleaf. The company says compatible Nanoleaf shapes can be integrated into the Philips Hue ecosystem with the Wall Light Module. Those devices will work with Hue’s scenes and automations within app control.

The app itself is also getting a couple of changes. First, Philips Hue on Android and iOS will get backup and restore functionality, so users don’t lose their scenes and automations if the app is deleted or they switch phones. The app will also start offering AI-generated scenes that work around specific user needs.

Both of those upgrades will roll out “beginning in fall 2026.”

The new Philips Hue Play Screen Sync will start at $119, while the Play HDMI sync box will be available for $149. Both are now available on Philips Hue’s website and retailers like Amazon.

title: MrBeast will try to survive ‘the planet’s most unforgiving landscapes’ using Gemini and Fitbit Air in deal with Google
snippet: Google has struck a deal with MrBeast, the most popular YouTuber, to promote Gemini and Google Health, with one of the first partnerships being a challenge in “the planet’s most unforgiving landscapes.” more…
fullText:
Google has struck a deal with MrBeast, the most popular YouTuber, to promote Gemini and Google Health, with one of the first partnerships being a challenge in “the planet’s most unforgiving landscapes.”

In a “multi-year partnership” that extends beyond YouTube, Google will work with MrBeast – aka Jimmy Donaldson – to promote Gemini and Google Health. This starts with a video going live on September 5 on the MrBeast channel that will see Jimmy and co racing through the jungle, desert, and the Arctic, relying on Gemini to help guide them through the challenge. Google says the Fitbit Air will also be integrated into an “upcoming challenge” of some kind.

An ad spot about Gemini will also feature Jimmy, showing how the AI assistant can be used to build out the channel’s infamous stunts.

Google explains:

	

As the first creator to reach 500 million YouTube subscribers, Jimmy Donaldson, better known as MrBeast, is always pushing the boundaries of what’s possible. Now, he’s tapping into Gemini to help him execute wilder concepts, showing his fans how they can use AI to help turn impossibly big ideas into reality. Along the way, he’ll also show how Google Health can support their daily fitness and wellness goals.

First up on September 5 is a new MrBeast video following Jimmy and his crew as they attempt to survive some of the most extreme and treacherous climates on Earth. Teams will race to navigate three of the planet’s most unforgiving landscapes — the jungle, the desert, and the Arctic — using Gemini to help them identify dangers, survive brutal weather changes, and stay one step ahead.

Beyond YouTube, keep an eye out for Jimmy’s upcoming spot in our newly launched Gemini campaign, where he’ll show how he uses the app as a partner to help him pull off the logistics of his signature, larger-than-life stunts. You’ll also see Jimmy integrate Fitbit Air into an upcoming challenge.

It’s far from the first time anyone has worked with MrBeast to market products. Samsung, as just one of many examples, partnered with the channel to use Galaxy phones for vlogging purposes back in 2023.
