title: These New Robot Vacuums, Mops, Mowers and Pool Cleaners Will Try to Convince Us They’re Maintenance-Free
snippet: Roborock’s new lineup at IFA 2026 is all about improving navigation and hands-free maintenance. I’ll be the judge.
fullText:
Roborock has offered some of the most unique and innovative robot vacuum models I’ve seen over the years. They’ve ranged from the arm-equipped Saros Z70, which I tested at home, to the stair-climbing Saros Rover we saw at CES earlier this year. At the 2026 IFA trade show in Berlin, the company is focusing on improving performance and perfecting the hands-free maintenance of the tried and true flagship robot vacuums, wet and dry mops, robot mowers and pool-cleaning robots.

The goal is to improve each model’s ability to handle the complexity of homes, yards and pools without requiring extensive human management and intervention to get over obstacles or self-clean.

“Our mission is about giving time back to our customers by automating and improving everyday tasks,” said Ricky Ma, president of Europe and Americas at Roborock, in a press statement. “Building smarter robots is just the means, not the goal. Every minute spent worrying about housework is a minute taken away from family, passions and personal well-being.”

I cover vacuums and home tech for CNET. While I’m here at IFA, I’m determined to seek out the most interesting tech that solves your most common cleaning problems. I’m excited to see the Saros 20 Neo, F25 Pro Turbo Combo and other devices in person on Wednesday. I’ll report back with my impressions later.

Saros 20 Flow Complete and Saros 20 Neo (Qrevo Edge 3 Pro in the US) 

The Saros 20 Flow comes with Roborock’s key features and impressive obstacle avoidance.Roborock

The Saros 20 Flow Complete is Roborock’s newest top-tier robot vacuum with all the key cleaning features you’d expect. It has a powerful 36,000 pa of suction and lidar navigation. Naturally, it comes with AI, allowing it to recognize over 300 types of obstacles, and Roborock says it can navigate easily in both well-lit and dark environments. 

It’s just 8.98 centimeters thick, which Roborock says makes it the slimmest robot vacuum on the market. The roller mop has 15 newtons of downward pressure, 240 rotations per minute and uses 16 pressurized water outlets to tackle tougher stains on hard floors. The pressurized water spraying is a feature I’ve seen on other robot vacuum models, as companies try to address the problem of dried stains in devices that aren’t suited for a lot of elbow grease.

Roborock

The robot also comes with dual-lifting side brushes to tackle edges. It has the AdaptLife system we’ve seen on other models, which allows it to cross double thresholds up to 8.8 cm. Like most flagship models. And it comes with a self-cleaning docking station that will wash and dry the mop, self-empty and dispense detergent. 

The Saros 20 Neo, called the Qrevo Edge 3 Pro in the US, is similar to the Flow, but is designed specifically to tackle more complex home layouts without requiring you to rescue the robot. It comes with the AdaptLift chassis 3.0 to clear double-layer thresholds of 8.8 cm. It’s even slimmer than the Flow at 7.95 cm, letting it fit under low-clearance furniture. It has an extended battery life, which Roborock says is enough to clean 350 square meters (around 3,767 square feet) in a single run. 

Roborock

In cleaning performance, it has 36,000 pa of suction and anti-tangle rollers to handle long pet hair. It also mops with 14 newtons of downward pressure and has a self-cleaning, self-emptying docking station.

Price and availability are yet to be confirmed, but Roborock says the Neo/Edge 3 Pro will be immediately available as of this writing. The Flow Complete is expected to launch in the US before October, with more details on price and availability to be shared later.

F25 Ultra Steam Gen 2 and F25 Pro Turbo Combo 

Wet and dry mops may not be as exciting as robot vacuums, but they’re having their moment this year as Roborock continues to update its lineup. The newest models are the F25 Ultra Steam Gen 2 and F25 Pro Turbo Combo. The Gen 2 Steam outputs 2.5 times as much steam as the previous generation, letting it handle stains and more greasy messes faster. Once preheated, Roborock says it can output the steam at 180 degrees Celsius in 30 seconds. 

It supports automatic cleaning adjustments for different flooring types, a feature I liked on the F25 Ultra. Roborock says it’s designed to fit under low furniture and has wheel assist to help you move it around smoothly. It has a robotic arm (not in the sense of the Saros Z70) that lets you get up against walls and edges and supports self-cleaning and drying. 

The F25 Pro Turbo Combo is meant to be the company’s jack-of-all-trades. Roborock calls it a five-in-one because it combines a wet and dry vacuum with a cordless vacuum in a single unit, letting it tackle both hard flooring and carpet for wet and dry cleaning. It has 25,000 pascals of suction, assisted wheels, and a scraper that keeps hair from getting tangled in the brush. I’m generally a big fan of the combo vacuums; they save you from buying multiple devices, but I’ll be curious to see how it measures up in our lab tests. 

The F25 Ultra Steam Gen 2 is expected to launch in the US on Sept. 28. We’re still waiting on details for the F25 Pro Turbo Combo.

RockNeo Q2 Lidar

Cunion

On the lawn care side, Roborock is coming with the RockNeo Q2 Lidar. It’s wire-free, with no need for a boundary wire or RTK beacon. Roborock says the lidar is sufficient to navigate diverse yards and surroundings and find its way through narrow areas. It can handle slopes up to 45% and passages as narrow as 60 centimeters. It has a three-blade cutting system that’s capable of 3 cm edge cutting. The mower itself is IPx6 waterproof.

The charging station has a built-in Wi-Fi amplifier, improving connectivity between the machine and the app and letting you manage mowing zones and cutting routines. There’s anti-theft protection built-in and support for Alexa and Google Home.

US availability and pricing for the RockNeo Q2 will be confirmed later.

RockAqua P1 

Summer’s drawing to an end, but Roborock’s RockAqua P1 is the company’s newest pool cleaner for next season. Roborock says it’s the first robotic pool cleaner that’s built to clean not just the pool floor, but also the walls, waterline and shallow platforms. That’s a significant improvement from other pool robots we’ve tested that often struggle with more complex pools or require you to handle steps or the waterline yourself. 

The P1 can handle more complex pool shapes, floor shapes and obstacles, like steps. It can clean platforms as shallow as 15 cm, and uses vision-based obstacle avoidance to identify drain covers and steps. 

In capabilities, it can handle fine debris, sand and large leaves with 6,800 gallons per hour suction power, a 4-liter debris basket, and dual filtration with 180 μm and 70 μm filters. It can automatically adjust suction based on the debris it encounters, including reducing it to avoid disturbing debris as it approaches. 

It has 3.5 hours of running time, letting it cover large pools and supports fast charging. US pricing and availability will be determined later. 

Editors’ note: Ajay Kumar’s travel costs for the IFA conference were covered by Roborock. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

title: Siri AI won’t be your friend, and here’s why that really matters
snippet: Elon University has partnered with The Washington Post to conduct what turned out to be a worrying survey about Americans viewing AI chatbots as virtual friends or therapists. The results very much vindicate Apple’s careful decision to ensure that Siri AI doesn’t encourage such pseudo-relationships … more…
fullText:
Elon University has partnered with The Washington Post to conduct what turned out to be a worrying survey about Americans viewing AI chatbots as virtual friends or therapists.

The results very much vindicate Apple’s careful decision to ensure that Siri AI doesn’t encourage such pseudo-relationships … 

The AI friendship findings

More than a quarter of Americans view AI chatbots in much the same way they might a close friend or therapist, according to The Washington Post.

Many talk to AI apps as they might a close friend or therapist […] 27% of Americans turn to AI chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Google’s Gemini with personal, emotional or social queries, according to a new poll [including] seeking entertainment, relationship advice, romantic chats, or connection when alone.

Among the people who said they used chatbots for personal or emotional queries or discussions, nearly 4 in 10 strongly or somewhat agreed that they sometimes talked to AI to feel less alone. Nearly a third said they consider the chatbot they use most often to be a friend.

While some of this usage may serve positive purposes, the concern is that having chatbots act as an emotional substitute for friendship and romance reduces the incentives to invest time and effort in establishing genuine human connections. It may lead to a downward spiral of increasing social isolation.

Siri AI does not encourage this

Apple execs Craig Federighi and Greg Joswiak said earlier this year that Siri AI will not act in this way.

Q: “So just to confirm, there are no AI girlfriends or boyfriends being created with the updated Siri AI?”

A: No, no, no. Quite the opposite. Because as you may know, if you use many of the existing chatbots, they’re really focused on engagement to a large degree. And sycophantic, right? They kind of want to pull you in. They might encourage you to reveal things about yourself and then use that as a basis to establish a connection.

And we view it quite the opposite. I mean, the way that we have designed Siri, Siri really wants to say, listen, that’s not what I’m here for, right? I’m here to help you. I can help you get things done. I can help you learn about the world. But if you try to engage Siri as a romantic partner, Siri is not up for that.

9to5Mac’s Take

I found the survey results extremely alarming, especially after listening to the excellent Suspicious Minds: Al and the Apocalypse podcast about AI-fueled delusions. The stance Apple is taking here is absolutely the right one.

title: Samsung is randomly deactivating some accounts for ‘security reasons’
snippet: A bizarre issue has left many Samsung Galaxy owners locked out of their Samsung accounts which were “deactivated for security reasons.” more…
fullText:
A bizarre issue has left many Samsung Galaxy owners locked out of their Samsung accounts which were “deactivated for security reasons.”

Over the past 24 hours or so, a number of Samsung Galaxy users have taken to the web with reports of being locked out of their Samsung accounts. A message appears saying that the account is “deactivated.”

Can’t sign in. Account deactivated for security reasons.

Dozens of users have reported the issue across Reddit threads and Samsung’s Community forums. Samsung hasn’t directly provided an explanation for the issue. This can have a pretty big impact on using a Galaxy device, especially if a user is invested in Samsung’s software ecosystem including apps like SmartThings, Wallet, and Find. 

Some users appear to have had success getting back into their account with the help of support, but it’s very hit or miss. 

	

While there’s no clear problem at play here, it does appear that alias email addresses may play a role – adding “+” or “.” to an address. One support representative apparently mentioned this and a number of those affected mentioned that they do indeed use an alias of their email address for their Samsung account. But not everyone affected uses an alias, so this is likely not the sole cause.

Samsung has yet to confirm the issue or comment on a fix beyond generic troubleshooting. We’ve reached out to Samsung for more information and will update this article when we hear back.

If you’re running into this problem, let us know in the comments below.

Thanks Evan!

title: Delivery Hero board backs Uber’s $15B takeover bid
snippet: If approved, the combined company would become one of the largest food delivery platforms in the world.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

12:25 PM PDT · September 2, 2026

Image Credits:John MACDOUGALL / AFP / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

Delivery Hero’s board has signed off on Uber’s $15 billion takeover offer and recommended shareholders approve the deal, which would create one of the largest on-demand food delivery platforms in the world.

After reviewing the offer, Delivery Hero’s supervisory and management boards said it was in the best interests of the company, its shareholders, employees, and other stakeholders. The boards also deemed that the price was “fair and adequate” and said the deal had the “potential to accelerate product innovation.”

The deal, if approved, would double Uber’s global footprint and make its delivery platform one of the largest in the world outside of China. It could also put Uber in a better position to compete with DoorDash and Just Eat Takeaway.

Uber, which was already the largest shareholder in Delivery Hero, set a minimum acceptance threshold of 50%, plus one share of Delivery Hero’s outstanding share capital. 

Prosus, another major shareholder, has agreed to sell its 17% stake in Delivery Hero as well, according to the announcement. Delivery Hero previously agreed to sell its businesses in 14 markets where Uber Eats already operates to New York-based investment firm SSW Partners for $1.6 billion.

The tie-up is the latest example of consolidation in the on-demand delivery industry. In the past 18 months, Uber agreed to acquire Turkey-based Getir for $335 million, Grab said it would buy Delivery Hero’s Foodpanda business in Taiwan for $600 million in cash, and DoorDash said it would pay $3.87 billion for the U.K.’s Deliveroo.

title: Apple iPhone 18 Pro Color Leak Claims Black Model Will Replace Silver This Year

fullText:
Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are expected to be unveiled at the company’s Sept. 9 launch event, and a new rumor appears to be firming up the three-color lineup for these phones.

title: Google Meet hardware dropping ChromeOS for Android
snippet: As we wait for consumer Googlebooks to launch, Google shared today that it is “transitioning [its] Google Meet hardware portfolio from ChromeOS to Android.” more…
fullText:
As we wait for consumer Googlebooks to launch, Google shared today that it is “transitioning [its] Google Meet hardware portfolio from ChromeOS to Android.”

Existing Google Meet hardware consists of touchscreen controllers, cameras, microphones, speakers, and what’s essentially a Chromebox to run scheduling software and the actual video conferencing suite.

Google is replacing ChromeOS with Android going forward. That said, “existing investments in ChromeOS devices are protected,” with full software support: “We will continue delivering security patches, stability updates, and ChromeOS releases for all Google Meet hardware running ChromeOS.” There are no changes to support timelines, with hardware continuing to work until 2030 for recent models. 

Hardware partners like Logitech, CTL, and Asus will “gradually end manufacturing and sales for ChromeOS-based hardware according to the following timelines.”

	

Logitech / CTL Google Meet Compute System: February 2027

ASUS Google Meet Compute System: April 2027

For customers looking to purchase ChromeOS devices to complement their existing fleet, particularly for large event spaces, we encourage you to purchase devices as soon as possible.

Google says Android for Google Meet hardware “provides several benefits”:

Device variety: Android-based room hardware offers a broader range of form factors, including compact all-in-one devices, video bars, and integrated room solutions. Whether equipping a focus room, collaborative huddle space, or boardroom, you have options to find the right fit.

Enterprise stability: Android-based devices deliver the performance, responsiveness, and stability you rely on with ChromeOS.

Hardware flexibility: Certified AOSP devices can run multiple video conferencing solutions, protecting your investment by allowing rooms to be repurposed without replacing equipment.

Long lifecycles: Devices certified for Google Meet are engineered for long-term reliability and predictable software support.

The company teases “several exciting Android devices intended for large-format spaces planned for 2027.”

title: Will Apple’s ‘revamped’ Health app with AI health coach debut next month?
snippet: Earlier this year, rumors were rampant about a revamped Health app coming to iOS 26.4. Then the project was delayed, and iOS 27 came and went, and the revamp still didn’t arrive. With the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 debuting next month, it’s worth asking: will we see the features debut alongside new hardware? more…
fullText:
Earlier this year, rumors were rampant about a revamped Health app coming to iOS 26.4. Then the project was delayed, and iOS 27 came and went, and the revamp still didn’t arrive.

With the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 debuting next month, it’s worth asking: will we see the features debut alongside new hardware?

Precedence

First and foremost, it’s worth going over why it’s probable that the features will debut in September. You might think “Shouldn’t all the software be unveiled in June?” – but there’s actually some precedence here.

Low Power Mode in watchOS 9, Sleep Apnea detection in watchOS 11, and Hypertension notifications in watchOS 26 were all features that weren’t unveiled until September despite not requiring the latest hardware.

So, for those reasons – it’s incredibly likely that Apple would wait until September to unveil its latest Health app upgrades, even if they don’t necessarily require the brand new Apple Watch.

There’s still time

Prior to WWDC27, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman warned that the new Health app upgrades, dubbed Project Mulberry, might not make an appearance at the WWDC keynote. Obviously, that now ended up being the case:

The Apple Health app is getting a range of new AI features that were originally planned for a comprehensive health coach service internally dubbed “Mulberry” that was scaled back. The upgrade, which includes improved blood sugar-related tracking and the ability to use a device camera to monitor a person’s workout, is not expected to arrive in the initial release of iOS 27. Apple may also announce these at a later date than WWDC.

Does this necessarily mean that Project Mulberry will for sure debut at the September keynote? No. That said, given the past feature unveils in September and the fact that we already knew it could be released later than WWDC, a September unveil feels somewhat likely, even if it ultimately ends up debuting in iOS 27.1 in October.

Feature recap

The rumors have been a bit wishy-washy regarding this feature set, since there are tons of variables at play. One of the things you may have heard was that there’d be a standalone Health+ service with videos from doctors. However, that plan was reportedly scaled back in favor of integrating the features into the usual Health app experience.

There are two very clear things though: there’ll be an AI health coach that gives you tips on your health based on health app data, and it’ll also have the ability to use your camera to give you real-time advice on workouts and other health-related tasks. Another key part of this upgrade is a new Health app design that makes it easier to make sense of all of the data.

Beyond that, we’ll have to wait and see. I, for one, am looking forward to having a much better way of making sense of my Apple Health data.

fullText:
Razer has just launched its new Prio game controller, a USB-C controller for your smartphone that folds down to the footprint of a credit card.

Available now, the Razer Prio’s claim to fame is that it’s very compact. 

Like countless other mobile game controllers, it attaches to either side of your phone and plugs in via USB-C, but when you’re not actively using it, the controller folds down into a size that’s roughly the same footprint as a credit card – around 10-15mm wider and taller. Despite the size, it still features tactile low-profile thumbsticks and dual bumpers and triggers, as well as a D-Pad and ABXY buttons. The thumbsticks avoid drift issues by using contactless sensors. 

	

Razer Prio is available today for $99.99 from the company’s online store, the same price as Kishi V3. Prio is also already available and shipping via Amazon.

title: OpenAI calls trade secret dispute ‘a mess of Apple’s own making’
snippet: Apple yesterday presented what it said was “shocking evidence” based on analysis of a MacBook owned by Chang Liu, a former employee who moved to OpenAI. The company is alleging that two of its former employees stole trade secrets relating to hardware design and more. The AI company hit back with its own legal filing, saying that the whole situation is “a mess of Apple’s own making” … more…
fullText:
Apple yesterday presented what it said was “shocking evidence” based on analysis of a MacBook owned by Chang Liu, a former employee who moved to OpenAI. The company is alleging that two of its former employees stole trade secrets relating to hardware design and more.

The AI company hit back with its own legal filing, saying that the whole situation is “a mess of Apple’s own making” …

The ongoing lawsuit is to determine whether Liu and Tang Tan stole confidential information acquired from their employment at Apple in order to help OpenAI develop an AI hardware device. In particular, it alleges that both engineers downloaded confidential engineering files after leaving the iPhone maker.

Apple was granted access to a MacBook belonging to Liu in order to carry out a forensic analysis to determine whether it held evidence of unlawful access to the company’s intellectual property. The firm yesterday submitted a court filing claiming it had found four “shocking” pieces of evidence backing its allegations.

In its own filing made the same day, Reuters reports that OpenAI doesn’t hold back.

Employees “can leave a company like Apple that has struggled to ⁠adopt ​AI and move to an exciting startup that builds innovative products,” ​OpenAI wrote. “Apple may not like those choices. But it cannot claim those choices are unlawful, and it cannot use its own sloppy ​procedures to blame others for its own mess.”

	

Specifically, it says the problems were caused by three issues:

Apple encourages employees to use personal iCloud accounts to access Apple documents

Departing employees aren’t given enough time to return company devices, transfer files back to the company, and hand over responsibilities

Former employees are contacted by their erstwhile team members for assistance after they have left, requiring them to access company information

9to5Mac’s Take

On the face of it, the evidence Apple provided yesterday does appear damning. OpenAI doesn’t seem to be denying that confidential Apple information was used by the company, but rather claiming that the iPhone maker failed to properly protect it.

However, while I’m not a lawyer, my understanding is that this could become a crucial argument – since companies can only claim information comprises a trade secret if they have taken appropriate steps to protect it. If OpenAI can show that Apple did not do so, then the AI company could prevail even if use of the information is proven.

title: iOS 27 breaks 15 years of muscle memory on iPhone and iPad
snippet: Since iOS 5 in 2011, the iPhone and iPad have included Notification Center, a central place to find alerts from various apps in chronological order. Starting with iOS 27, Apple is making a major change to how users open Notification Center on iPhone and iPad. iOS 27 is currently in beta, and the behavior has changed slightly between the first two releases. However, eight developer betas so far show this change will ship this month — even if I’d change it. more…
fullText:
Since iOS 5 in 2011, the iPhone and iPad have included Notification Center, a central place to find alerts from various apps in chronological order.

Starting with iOS 27, Apple is making a major change to how users open Notification Center on iPhone and iPad.

iOS 27 is currently in beta, and the behavior has changed slightly between the first two releases. However, eight developer betas so far show this change will ship this month — even if I’d change it.

Siri AI takes over the swipe gesture for a lot of the iPhone and iPad top edge

Opening Notification Center is unchanged on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 by default. However, enabling Siri AI changes a key swipe gesture on both iPhone and iPad.

One of the many ways of invoking Siri AI, once enabled, is by swiping down from the center of the top edge of your iPhone or iPad display. This previously opened Notification Center.

You can still access Notification Center by swiping down from the top-left corner once Siri AI is enabled. Alerts now animate in from the top left corner. This is a way to point users toward Notification Center’s smaller surface area.

Apple is greatly prioritizing Siri AI access in iOS 27. The majority of the top edge is devoted to invoking the new Siri experience.

The last time Apple made a change to accessing Notification Center came when Control Center moved from a swipe up gesture from the bottom to a top-right corner swipe down gesture on iPhone X. Apple later unified this experience across devices.

Notifications now live in the top left corner

Now it’s Notification Center’s turn to be put in the corner. On iPadOS 27 beta 1 in particular, the area above Home screen app icons was pretty much devoted to invoking Siri AI. The area for opening Notification Center actually shrank if you disable displaying AM/PM or the date.

	

Apple improved this with iPadOS 27 beta 2, creating a more uniform region on either side. It’s roughly the size of two app columns with Notification Center on the left and Control Center on the right. The rest is for invoking Siri. 

After 15 years of muscle memory, it’ll take some time to determine if this change is worth it or something that should be reconsidered. In the meantime, early feedback sounds overwhelmingly positive around Apple’s new Siri AI system. Hearing that Siri is good now will also take some getting used to, I’m sure.

After months of using the new behavior, I’m certain I’d toggle it off if there were a setting to do so. Since there’s no option to disable invoking Siri from the top middle swipe down, the only thing to do is build new muscle memory around avoiding the center.

iOS 27 is currently available as a developer and public beta. The official release is expected this month.

title: Instagram cracking down on accounts that feature AI-generated influencers
snippet: As AI slop continues to dominate the web, Instagram is cracking down on accounts that leverage AI-generated influencers by threatening to restrict their reach. more…
fullText:
As AI slop continues to dominate the web, Instagram is cracking down on accounts that leverage AI-generated influencers by threatening to restrict their reach.

In a blog post, Instagram details that its “AI creator” label for accounts is now going to say “AI-generated profile,” better reflecting that the account is not just using AI, but that viewers are interacting with an influencer that is entirely AI-generated. 

Accounts that were using the “AI creator” label will have a chance to review the status and have it removed if it no longer fits their content. 

The bigger change, though, is that Instagram will actively crack down on accounts that don’t use the label at all if they are using “AI-generated influencers.” This includes not showing content in recommendations such as the “For You” page. 

	

Instagram explains:

For unlabeled profiles that feature an AI-generated person, creators can and should apply the label by editing their profile and toggling on AI-generated profile. The label will then begin to appear on their profile and alongside their content if their specific media doesn’t already have a label indicating that it was created or edited with AI. Creators who proactively add the AI-generated profile label will not see a change to their profile’s reach.

Adding the label or appealing the decision can reverse the impact, but this is a considerable change on Instagram’s part, especially as AI-generated content has become incredibly prevelant on both Instagram and Facebook, both Meta-operated platforms.

title: Dropbox breach seemingly caused by egregious authentication failure [U]
snippet: Multiple Dropbox users have been emailed by the cloud storage company to advise them that a security breach saw unauthorised access to their account. Update: the company has said that about 5,000 accounts were compromised, with files downloaded from around 1,500 of them. The root cause appears to be a lack of authentication by Dropbox when attackers created a single sign-on option through a third-party company … more…
fullText:
Multiple Dropbox users have been emailed by the cloud storage company to advise them that a security breach saw unauthorised access to their account. Update: the company has said that about 5,000 accounts were compromised, with files downloaded from around 1,500 of them.

The root cause appears to be a lack of authentication by Dropbox when attackers created a single sign-on option through a third-party company … 

Developer Yoni Levy posted a copy of the email he received on X.

We are writing to let you know that we’ve observed unauthorized access to your Dropbox account between August 4 and August 21, 2026. While our logs show no evidence that your files were viewed or downloaded, we want to share with you what happened, what we are doing about it, and what additional steps you can take.

Other Dropbox users reported receiving the same email in which the company said it resulted from a problem with a single sign-on (SSO) option using Lenovo IDs.

Dropbox partners with Lenovo as an identity provider so that users can log in to their Dropbox accounts using verified Lenovo IDs. While you may not have an existing Lenovo ID, our investigation determined that an issue with Lenovo’s email verification process allowed an unauthorized party to register a Lenovo ID using your email address and then use that Lenovo ID to log into the Dropbox account associated with that email address.

However, while Dropbox claims the flaw was in Lenovo’s email verification process, the bigger issue appears to be that Dropbox itself did not require users to use their existing login to verify the new SSO, as The CyberSec Guru reports.

Recon/selection: The attacker compiles target email addresses (breach corpora, LinkedIn, customer lists — email addresses are effectively public data).

Rogue IdP enrollment: The attacker registers a Lenovo ID as victim@example.com. No inbox access is needed because Lenovo’s verification step is missing or bypassable. The display name is set to something disposable — one victim who reclaimed the rogue account found the name “John Madden,” the late NFL broadcaster, a strong tell of bulk, low-effort registration.

Federated sign-in: The attacker clicks “Continue with Lenovo” on Dropbox. Lenovo’s authorization server issues a token whose email claim matches the victim’s Dropbox account.

Implicit account linking: Dropbox resolves the email claim to the existing account and mints a session. No password prompt, no step-up, no “link this new identity?” consent. From Dropbox’s perspective, a trusted IdP had already vouched for the address.

9to5Mac’s Take

While there was certainly a failure to verify email addresses at the Lenovo end, it would not have done any harm if Dropbox had authenticated the linked ID before it could be used to sign in. Failing to do so is an egregious fault.

The company has now fixed the flaw and expired all sessions previously ‘authenticated’ through a Lenovo ID.

If you don’t already have two-factor authentication enabled for Dropbox, it is highly recommended to change this immediately.

snippet: Despite their increasingly-thin designs, Samsung’s foldables have held up well to torture tests that include more bending than you’d ever see in real life. But it seems the Galaxy Z Fold 8 UItra might finally be too thin, as it’s the first mainstream Samsung foldable that’s died in a bend test. more…
fullText:
Despite their increasingly-thin designs, Samsung’s foldables have held up well to torture tests that include more bending than you’d ever see in real life. But it seems the Galaxy Z Fold 8 UItra might finally be too thin, as it’s the first mainstream Samsung foldable that’s died in a bend test.

The Galaxy Z Fold 7 showed that, yes, Samsung could actually make a thin foldable. And for good measure, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra pushes that a step further with another slight reduction in thickness. 

In the usual torture test from YouTube channel JerryRigEverything, the Fold 8 Ultra holds up just about as well as anyone would expect. Durable outer display, easily scratching inside, and some deeply unsettling crunching noises when dust gets into the hinge. But it’s the bend test that’s out of the ordinary here.

Save for the very-limited Galaxy Z TriFold, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is the first of Samsung’s foldables to break during a bend test. It’s no spectacular failure, though. The hinge and frame both stay intact; the inner display just… dies.

	

It’s interesting that the Ultra fails here despite the wider Fold 8 living through the same bend test.

fullText:
Thomas Ricker

 

is a deputy editor and Verge co-founder with a passion for human-centric cities, e-bikes, and life as a digital nomad. He’s been a tech journalist for 20 years.

Detail-preserving optical lens shift is not something you expect to find on an ultra-short throw projector running Google TV, but that’s exactly what you’ll find inside of Awol Vision’s new LuxVision. It also promises to produce an incredibly bright (6000 ISO Lumens) 4K 120Hz image measuring 120 inches when placed just 7.5 inches from the wall.

The vertical lens shift is the star here. Most UST projectors use digital trickery to manipulate the image onto the wall or screen behind it. The LuxVision can raise and lower the output optically to preserve the detail in the 4K image without having to move the projector or resort to keystone correction. That makes this, like all USTs, a possible TV replacement if you’ve got enough cash to offset your hatred for ugly black monoliths. LuxVision is available in a number of colors and trims for that very reason.

Awol Vision is pitching the LuxVision at sports fans by playing up the fluidity of the 4K 120Hz display, which is still a rarity in projectors. It’s also targeting gamers by baking in Dolby Vision Gaming HDR, ALLM, VRR, and an input lag of around 1ms. You also get 3x HDMI 2.1 ports, 1x DisplayPort, and HDMI Multiview to view up to four sources simultaneously.

As you might have guessed, these specs won’t come cheap. It’ll list for $5,999 at launch, sometime “around October.” And that’s before you shell out another $1,000 or so for an ALR screen that can dramatically enhance the viewing experience. Starting September 5th, Awol Vision is offering discounts for anyone willing to preorder the LuxVision ahead of the reviews.

fullText:
Welcome to Indie App Spotlight. This is a weekly 9to5Mac series where we showcase the latest apps in the indie app world. If you’re a developer and would like your app featured, get in contact.

If you lose track of things you’d like to reference later, Laytr might be a nice solution for you. All of us save things all over the place, whether that be browser bookmarks, built-in bookmarking features within apps, taking a screenshot to hopefully find later, or just leaving a tab open and hoping we find it again later. Laytr aims to be a nice all-in-one solution for keeping track of your digital bookmarks.

Highlights

Laytr offers an incredibly organized UI for keeping tabs on everything. It works with the native iOS share sheet, so when you find something, just hit share and click on Laytr. After that, you can set what to categorize it as, as well as when you want to be reminded again.

Within the app, there are three core tabs. The first one is the Now tab, where it highlights things you need to see imminently. There’s Timeline, which lets you scroll ahead and see things based on the date you set the reminder for, and Library, where you can see everything you’ve ever saved, both in categories or grouped together. Beyond that, you can also search.

One differentiating feature is that there’s no sync, even with iCloud, and no accounts. Everything lives on your device in its own separate bubble, and your data will never live on someone else’s server.

Download the app

Laytr is available for free on the App Store for iPhone models running iOS 17 and later. You can use the app for free, but for unlimited access you’ll need a $1.99/month or $14.99/year subscription. There’s also a discount on lifetime, which normally fetches $39.99 but can be had for just $24.99 for early adopters.

Features like searching and exporting will never be limited by the paywall, so even if you decide to unsubscribe later, the app will remain usable.

title: One of Our Top Robot Vacuum Brands Is Diving into Pool Care
snippet: The RockAqua P1 made its splashdown at IFA 2026 in Berlin, and we saw it first.
fullText:
Roborock, one of the flashiest home robot makers, is taking the plunge. The Beijing-based brand, known for its super-smart robot vacuums, including models with robotic grabbing arms and stair-climbing capabilities, has launched its first-ever robotic pool cleaner. 

We saw it first at IFA Berlin.

On a crowded showroom floor, we got a look at Roborock’s small and colorful new pool cleaner. Dubbed the RockAqua P1, this autonomous underwater vacuum is engineered to clean pool floors, walls, waterlines and shallow platforms. 

Roborock has entered the pool-care conversation with the launch of the RockAqua P1 at IFA.

Its adaptive cleaning path, a feature prominent in Roborock’s indoor vacuums, allows the robot to navigate pools of different shapes and depths. Vision-based obstacle avoidance identifies obstacles such as drain covers and steps, helping reduce interruptions during cleaning.

	

			

	

			

									

						8 Best Robot Pool Cleaners, All Tested by CNET					

							

		

While obstacle avoidance is useful, the ability to track down debris in a pool using AI cognition, as our top-rated Aiper Scuba V3 does, is even more impressive. So far, it doesn’t look like Roborock’s entry into the pool-cleaner category offers a comparable debris-detection feature.

What the RockAqua P1 lacks in proactive leaf, bug, and stone hunting, it makes up for with a lot of suction power. The robot delivers a suction rate of 6,800 gallons per hour, placing it in the same class as some of the most powerful pool-cleaning robots from well-established brands. Still, our lab testing shows that raw power doesn’t necessarily translate to better cleaning.

Roborock’s first-ever pool vac can adjust its suction strategically to better capture debris.Tara Brown/CNET

One particularly interesting feature is the robot’s ability to adjust its suction depending on the situation. According to Roborock, when it encounters larger debris, the robot reduces suction to prevent the water flow from disturbing the debris and pushing it out of the cleaning path. As it gets closer, it increases suction to capture the debris.

Roborock’s first pool cleaner runs for up to 3.5 hours on a full charge, which is average for high-end models. When a cleaning cycle is complete, the robot rests on the water’s surface. That’s a useful touch, since some pool cleaners remain at the bottom and have to be hauled out manually. The surface-resting design should make the RockAqua P1 easier to retrieve for emptying and recharging.

As of now, the RockAqua P1 is set for release in the European market only, with a rollout to the US still in question.

title: The Weirdest and Wackiest Tech We Found at IFA 2026
snippet: From AI intimate companions to a smartphone for your dog, here’s what raised our eyebrows the most at this year’s IFA.
fullText:
Some tech at IFA was much more unusual than the rest. Here’s what caught our eye.Govee

IFA is in full swing, and the Berlin expo has gathered advanced tech from across the globe to show off, from all-new vacuum features to ultra-advanced AI ecosystems ready to help manage your home. Then there are the products that made us go, “…Huh.”

When tech companies are throwing everything they’ve got at IFA, things can get a little weird. Here’s the wackiest tech we spotted, what it’s supposed to do, and how useful we think it could be out in the real world.

Govee’s mood-reading sky light

Govee’s mood-interpreting light may not be as far-fetched as you think.Govee

Govee has long been at the forefront of strange home lighting creations, from literal curtains of light to spread across your garage to table lamps that look more like alien artifacts. Now Govee is showing off one of its oddest products yet: a dome-like ceiling light made to mimic the sky while being “mood-responsive.”

In this case, mood-responsive means you can use Govee’s AI to talk about your mood or how you’re feeling, and the Govee app will come up with ceiling light color schemes to match. But the light can also create a specific blue wavelength designed to evoke blue skies and natural daylight.

Too weird to work? Not as weird as you may think. I’ve tested Govee’s AI before, and you really can generate lighting patterns based on your mood or random musings. But Govee already has so many lighting scenes in its app that I didn’t find it very practical — although definitely fun. I wonder how well it will work with a full ceiling light.

SwitchBot’s AI shirt pin, the MindClip

SwitchBot’s AI clip sort of…spies on everyone around you.SwitchBot

If you thought AI was already in everything, just wait: SwitchBot is announcing the launch of its AI shirt device, the MindClip, at IFA. It’s made to clip onto your shirt pocket, collar, nearby strap or even belt. Once in place, it, well, essentially listens to everything that happens within a 3-meter radius for up to 20 hours and saves it for you.

The MindClip can recognize people by their voices and summarize conversations or events, ostensibly to help you with planning after a busy day. As far as AI goes, it’s no spying Meta glasses, but it is fairly invasive, especially for strangers you may be chatting with.  

Too weird to work? Interestingly, this isn’t the first time we’ve seen an AI pin, although it is the smallest and least distracting version I’ve spotted. The problem is that none of them really took off, and some companies even pivoted to an entirely different product. So yes, it’s too weird to work for now, but maybe the rumored AI capabilities in Apple’s AirPods will be an exception.

The AI-powered companion doll from Lovense

Lovense’s updated AI companion doll also made an appearance at IFA.Lovense

Singaporean intimacy and sex toy company Lovense has brought the latest version of its AI “companion doll” to IFA, aiming to make it more lifelike than ever before. In addition to talking, remembering past facts and adjusting its personality, the silicone doll can blink, smile and look when called by its custom name. Users can also chat with the doll at a distance via a phone app and set up roleplay scenarios, if they prefer.

Too weird to work? Yes, the age of AI sex dolls is here. But it’s such an eclectic — and expensive (between $4,000 and $8,000) — proposition, this one is only for those with very specific tastes and a, ahh, particular relationship with AI. For others, Lovense also debuted several more conventional, AI-free toys.

A Eufy sensor that asks if you fell down

Eufy’s new sensor has a very, very specific purpose in the home.Eufy

When today’s home sensors can do nearly anything from recognizing when dogs bark to knowing when someone is tampering with a mailbox, it may sound strange to make a sensor specifically to say, “Oops, it looks like you fell down!” But that’s just what Anker’s Eufy brand has done.

There’s method behind this madness. The wall sensor uses a combo of algorithms and presence sensing with mmWave technology, no cameras necessary. It’s made to help those aging in place or living in rest homes without creating privacy concerns. The sensor even supports two-way audio, so family members or nurses can check in if they get an alert about a potential fall.

Quick note: As Anker consolidates its brand names, Eufy products are staying with us, but the Eufy name may not be around forever, so keep that in mind when shopping.

Too weird to work? In this case, not at all. I’ve already seen mmWave technology tap into Wi-Fi signals to help those aging in place, although Eufy’s sensor is the first I’ve seen that focuses on falls and enables two-way audio for a quick checkup. It’s a strong use of the technology.

			

			

							
		

	

		

			Best DIY Home Security Systems of 2026: Install Them Yourself
		

					

Dodge installation fees and take security into your own hands with these super smart security kits.

						

		

A smartphone for your pet

The Petphone certainly makes a lot of claims about AI pet powers.Petpogo

Ucloudlink has brought the newest version of its award-winning PetPhone to IFA this year, showing a world where cats and dogs have their own smartphone, too. Sort of.

The Petpogo PetPhone is technically a smart pet collar, and we’ve reviewed many of those. But this version comes with two-way audio to talk to your pet with an app and AI features that interpret behavior and motion so pets can theoretically initiate a call themselves, as well as emotion analysis of barks, meows and other actions. It also supports more traditional capabilities like tracking and geofencing, and it alerts pet parents to out-of-routine behaviors.

Too weird to work? No AI features can accurately interpret specific barks or meows into moods and feelings. That’s (currently) nonsense. And trying to get your pet to “call” you with specific behaviors sounds dubious at best. So most of the innovations here are too weird, but the underlying collar functionality looks usable.

These headphones that turn into a Bluetooth speaker

TDM’s Bluetooth speaker headphone hybrid is confusing.TDM

TDM is showing off its very unique Neo headphones, with a literal twist. In normal mode, they look like a typical pair of wireless headphones. But twist and collapse the earcups, and they form into a small Bluetooth speaker with up to 8 hours of music playback. The dual-device comes with an aux port, a USB-C charging port and a carrying case.

Too weird to work? When was the last time you saw someone with headphones and thought, “What a pleasant, private music experience that person is having, I wish there was a way for them to share it with all the people nearby?” Nope. No one likes it when you play music out loud in public spaces, especially when the same device could let you listen privately. I’m calling these headphones too weird to work.

A soundwave-creating smart bed

Amada’s acoustic mattress claims many different applications.Amada

Amada brought a fascinating mattress to IFA called the Soundwave Smart Mattress. Yes, it connects to a phone app. And yes, it really does produce soundwaves or at least a “vibroacoustic experience” with vibration modes for pre-sleep relaxation, meditation, focus and recharging. I’m not sure how vibration is supposed to help with those things, but CNET health expert Anna Gragert told me vibration therapy does have applications for recovery and disease treatment. The bed is made of polyurethane foam and polyester fabric, with a four-pin power connector.

Too weird to work? Well, Magic Fingers did have their day in hotel rooms across the US, but that day ended pretty fast. I don’t know if a bed with good vibrations is what the average home is looking for, but if you’ve tried it and it works for you, this could be a shakingly good upgrade.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Tyler Lacoma
						

						

							Editor / Home Security and Smart Home						
					

											

								

											Tyler has worked on, lived with and tested all types of smart home and security technology for over a dozen years, explaining the latest features, privacy tricks, and top recommendations.
With degrees in Business Management, Literature and Technical Writing, Tyler takes every opportunity to play with the latest AI technology, push smart devices to their limits and occasionally throw cameras off his roof, all to find the best devices to trust in your life. He always checks with the renters (and pets) in his life to see what smart products can work for everyone, in every living situation. 
Living in beautiful Bend, Oregon gives Tyler plenty of opportunities to test the latest tech in every kind of weather and temperature. But when not at work, he can be found hiking the trails, trying out a new food recipe for his loved ones, keeping up on his favorite reading, or gaming with good friends.

title: You’re Addicted to Your Phone. Admitting That Is the First Step
snippet: More than of us say they overuse their smartphones, according to a Pew survey.
fullText:
You pick up your phone for a quick read, and suddenly an hour has disappeared. Sound familiar? 

More than half of adults say they use their phones excessively, according to a Pew Research Center survey conducted earlier this summer. Of the nearly 10,000 respondents, all 18 and older, 53% said they use smartphones too much, and 36% say they use their phones “about the right amount.”

The younger the people were, the more they felt they had overused phone use — 70% among those aged 18 to 29 and 64% among those aged 30 to 49. About 42% of the 18 to 29 group said they were on their phones “almost constantly.”

Digital marketing platform Semrush estimates that people worldwide average 4 hours and 37 minutes per day on the phone — 5 hours, 16 minutes in the US — and check their phones an average of 58 times per day.

Put another way, 5 hours on your phone each day adds up to 76 full 24-hour days a year. Start Jan. 1 at midnight when the new year begins, and you won’t put your phone down until around St. Patrick’s Day.

I’m assuming these numbers aren’t very surprising, considering we use our phones for everything from shopping and reading the news to texting, scrolling social media and playing games. Once we get accustomed to having instant gratification for our finances, communication and work, it’s hard to break the cycle. But as more of us realize the consequences, we’re starting to take action. 

Risks of too much device

Excessive phone use can have tragic consequences. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports that 3,208 people were killed in 2024 in auto accidents caused by distracted driving, which includes drivers talking or texting on the phone.

“Sending or reading a text takes your eyes off the road for 5 seconds,” the NHTSA reports. “At 55 mph, that’s like driving the length of an entire football field with your eyes closed.”

First Aid for Life, a UK-based first-aid training provider, said 41% in the UK have suffered some type of accident related to phone use. Wikipedia even has a gruesome list of selfie-related injuries and deaths.

Anxiety, stress, depression, social isolation, feelings of inadequacy, low self-esteem and even thoughts of suicide and self-harm can all arise from being on devices and social media too much, according to research from Columbia University’s department of psychiatry.

The main downside of excessive screen time in the survey was reduced sleep, with 41% reporting that phone use affected how much they slept. And 34% said phone use hurt productivity, as compared to 30% who said it helped.

Try this one trick

In the Pew study, 45% said they had tried to reduce their phone use over the previous year, and 46% had not. Of those trying to cut back, only 25% rated their attempts as extremely or very successful, and 52% said they were somewhat successful. 

For people using iPhones, there is a trick you can try to reduce screen time, says CNET senior writer Zachary McAuliffe.

“Try hiding iPhone apps in a folder in your App Library,” McAuliffe said. “This could prevent you from mindlessly opening apps when you’re bored, since there are more roadblocks to get to those apps. I’ve hidden a few apps on my device for this reason, and I forget I have them. Which is a nice reminder that I need to delete a few apps that I don’t use.”

CNET also has a list of five effective tech gadgets and apps to get you off that doomscrolling hamster wheel. Brick, our Editors’ Choice, is a locking device that lets you block certain apps with the press of a button and includes a timer that shows how long you’ve gone without looking at the phone.

You can also check out our recommendations for the best phone settings to stop doomscrolling.

title: Apple tells Mac App Store developers they can now drop Intel support
snippet: Apple started informing developers today that universal macOS apps on the Mac App Store that require macOS 13 or later can now drop support for Intel-based Macs. more…
fullText:
Apple started informing developers today that universal macOS apps on the Mac App Store that require macOS 13 or later can now drop support for Intel-based Macs.

In the email, Apple says:

We’re reaching out to let you know that universal macOS apps on the Mac App Store that require macOS 13 or later can now remove support for Intel-based Mac computers.

By removing support for Intel-based Mac computers, you can simplify your development and optimize your download and on-device size.

To remove Intel support, update your app build settings to “arm64” only. Then rebuild and submit your app to the Mac App Store.

Previously, developers were required to offer Intel compatibility. With today’s change, developers can drop support for Intel-based Macs. Intel users, however, can continue using the last version of the app compatible with their machine.

The changes come as macOS 27 Golden Gate drops support for Intel-powered Macs altogether. Apple also announced last year that Rosetta 2, the software that translates Intel apps for Apple Silicon, will be discontinued after macOS 27 (with some exceptions for for certain games).

title: HomeKit Weekly: Linkind’s Smart Light Stick brings flame effects with Matter support
snippet: “Flame effects” is not something I’d used before in a smart bulb, so this was a super interesting concept to me. Linkind’s Smart Light Stick aims to bring the idea of a “live flame” to a smart bulb, and it works with Apple Home out of the box thanks to Matter. more…
fullText:
“Flame effects” is not something I’d used before in a smart bulb, so this was a super interesting concept to me. Linkind’s Smart Light Stick aims to bring the idea of a “live flame” to a smart bulb, and it works with Apple Home out of the box thanks to Matter.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

The Light Stick is an E26 bulb, so it screws into a standard light socket, just like any other bulb in your lamp or ceiling fan. The pitch for the Linkind Smart Light Stick here isn’t just “another color bulb.” It’s a bulb built specifically around dynamic lighting effects, with flame simulation as the main feature.

The flame effects

Instead of a single flicker pattern, Linkind lets you independently adjust flame size, brightness, flicker speed, and motion type.  You can dial it down to something closer to soft candlelight, or push it toward a more intense, fiery look, depending on the room and the mood you’re aiming for.

Beyond flame effects, the bulb ships with more than 120 presets, including sunset glows, lava-inspired motion, and Christmas scenes. I kinda always take preset counts with a grain of salt, since these numbers are often padded with minor variations to inflate them, but the range described here at least covers many of your most varied use cases rather than just 120 shades of slightly different color effects.

Where Apple Home fits in

The bulb works with Amazon Alexa, Apple Home, and Google Home via Matter. That gets you the core functionality, on and off, brightness, and color in the Home app, alongside the rest of your Apple Home gear.

It’s worth being clear about what Matter does and doesn’t cover here, though. The deeper customization options, like the flame control, will live in Linkind’s own AiDot app rather than being fully exposed through Apple Home’s interface. That’s not the fault of Linkind, but rather the limitations of this category of Matter accessory at the moment. You get basic on/off control and automation integration through Apple Home, and you use the manufacturer’s app to actually design a scene.

Wrap up on the Linkind Smart Light Stick

If you just want a bulb that turns on and off via Apple Home, this is overkill; you can spend less elsewhere. If you want a genuinely cool light for a lamp or accent fixture, something that can go from a calm living room light to a full flame effect for a party, the Light Stick is one of the more feature-rich options I’ve seen, and the Matter support means it won’t be siloed away from the rest of your smart home.

You can grab it from Amazon.

title: M6 MacBook Pro: Three new upgrades launching this fall
snippet: Apple has a new M6 MacBook Pro launching this fall with a 14-inch screen and the current industrial design. Now that the M6 chip has officially been unveiled, here are three upgrades to expect from the new MacBook Pro. more…
fullText:
Apple has a new M6 MacBook Pro launching this fall with a 14-inch screen and the current industrial design. Now that the M6 chip has officially been unveiled, here are three upgrades to expect from the new MacBook Pro.

#1: Dual 16-core Neural Engine

If AI is in any way significant to your workflows—and with macOS 27, it will be for even more users—then the M6 MacBook Pro could be a big upgrade.

That’s because the M6 chip includes a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, up from the standard 16-core version available in M5 and prior. Per Apple:

M6 also introduces a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, providing up to 2x the peak compute over previous generations to make on-device AI workflows run even faster. System frameworks can automatically utilize both engines simultaneously, enabling applications to see faster model execution.

#2: 12-core CPU and GPU with powerful new cores

The base M6 chip offers a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU. Both are solid upgrades over the M5, which was limited to 10 cores each.

M6’s new CPU cores are especially interesting, as Apple is bringing three distinct core types to its base chip for the first time. It has 2 super cores, 4 performance cores, and 6 efficiency cores. Here’s what Apple says about each core:

Super cores: “blaze through single-threaded workloads”

Performance cores: “use less power and join the super cores to run demanding multithreaded workloads”

Efficiency cores: “handle everyday background tasks”

Previously only M5 Pro and M5 Max—and now M5 Ultra—provided super cores and performance cores in a single chip. But now these Pro-level capabilities are available for standard M6 users. 

#3: Major efficiency gains to likely improve battery life

M6 is the first Apple chip built on a new 2nm process. And the company says that brings the benefit of “a major leap in performance and power efficiency.”

Currently the only product with an M6 is the new Mac mini, which doesn’t run on a battery.

But in the MacBook Pro, MacBook Air, and other upcoming M6 products, the new chip’s “major leap” in power efficiency is likely to enable longer battery life.

Apple could always opt to shrink the physical battery to offer comparable performance as before, but here’s hoping it uses M6’s improved efficiency to deliver better battery life instead.

snippet: Anker announces the Sleep Earbuds 4 Pro at IFA, along with a stylish bedside sleep speaker, a hearing aid and a bunch of headphones.
fullText:
Last month, I took two back-to-back long-haul flights in economy that took me overnight from Asia to the UK. On paper, it sounded like a nightmare, and I was dreading it. But in the end, I managed to get a total of 7 hours of sleep — 5 of them on the first flight, which departed at 2 a.m.

I credit Anker’s Soundcore Sleep A30 earbuds, which drowned out all of the cabin noise around me and were also comfy enough to sleep in. I’ve been searching for this magic combination for a while now, and I finally found it in the A30s.

On Thursday at IFA in Berlin, Anker announced an upgrade to this holy grail product — the Sleep Earbuds 4 and Sleep Earbuds 4 Pro. The company says it’s made the earbuds even smaller, minimizing the 3D ergonomic design for even cozier sleeping. The Sleep 4 Pro also comes with a touchscreen case, allowing you to set alarms, play relaxing sounds and check insights all without touching your phone.

A key feature that sets the Pro model apart from the base model is what Anker calls a “track-assess-adjustment system.” This uses the headphones’ built-in sensors to measure various factors, including PPG, heart rate and HRV and adjust the audio to find the best sleep sounds for you to have the most effective sleep.

The Earbuds 4 will be available in October, with the Earbuds 4 Pro following soon after in November — though pricing is not yet available.

Anker’s sleek sleep speaker would look at home on my bedside table.

Anker is further building out its sleep ecosystem with a pair of stylish bedside speakers, which it also announced at IFA. The SleepLab will lull you to sleep with soft music and a nightlight, whereas the SleepLap Pro uses radar to track your sleep, heart rate and breathing, then play tailored audio to help you fall asleep and stay asleep — all with no wearables required.

The speakers feature a warm, circular lamp that almost appears to float within a wider cream circle. It looks like a thoughtfully designed piece of kit that I know I’d be happy to have on my bedside table. Anker isn’t sharing pricing or availability at this stage, but says no phone or subscription is required.

Anker headphones and a hearing aid

In May, Anker announced its first neural-net compute-in-memory AI audio chip called Thus, which it’s now put into a slew of new audio products.

Anker’s IFA headphone lineup is powered by its AI audio Thus chip.

The Anker Soundcore AeroClip 2 Pro is more than a pair of clip-on earbuds — the product is actually an AI note-taker that can capture online meetings and calls, transcribing them and providing summaries (not unlike the newly announced Plaud One headphones). There’s no launch date for the AeroClip 2 Pro right now, but there is a price — it will be $230.

Anker is really emphasizing clear call quality in its new audio device lineup. It’s listed as a major selling point of both the over-ear Soundcore Space 2 Pro and the Soundcore Liberty Buds 2. The Space 2 Pro comes with immersive adaptive active noise cancellation and 60 hours of listening time (30 hours with ANC on and 20 hours of talk time). The Libery Buds 2, meanwhile, pack six-sensor full-band ANC, which Anker promises will offer pure silence and block chaos so you can focus fully.

Both models will be available starting Sept. 22, with the Space2 Pro priced at $200 and the Liberty Buds 2 at $130.

The final audio product Anker unveiled at IFA is a little different and won’t be for everyone, but it will prove hugely useful to a select group. The Anker RIC Hearing Aids, also powered by the Thus chip, offer what the company describes as a clinical-grade hearing aid experience.

Anker’s hearing aid doesn’t have an on-sale date just yet.

The device will drown out unnecessary noise and amplify the voice you actually want to hear. Four beamforming microphones will lock onto the voice of the person you’re talking with, and the Thus chip will run 40 billion operations per second to isolate the sound.

There’s no pricing or availability details for the RIC Hearing Aids just yet, but it’s impressive to see Anker use its proprietary tech to develop an accessibility solution. The device will offer 12 hours of battery time, or 36 hours with the case, and 5 minutes of fast charging will give 2 hours of battery life.

Editors’ note: Katie Collins’ travel costs for the IFA conference were covered in part by Xiaomi. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

title: Circular’s New Smart Ring Brings Mobile Payments to Your Finger
snippet: The Circular Ring 3 Pro and Slim add NFC payments and haptic feedback, and still don’t require subscriptions for its core health features and AI coach.
fullText:
Circular is putting mobile payments at your fingertips with its new Circular Ring 3 series. Announced at IFA, the consumer tech show in Berlin, the Circular Ring 3 Pro and Circular Ring 3 Slim are bringing more smartwatch-like capability to the ring category.

Both models add contactless payments to Circular’s existing health tracking and bring back the haptic vibration feature from the original Circular Ring. That means the rings can buzz your finger for app notifications, medication reminders and health alerts without a screen or phone as the middle man.

The screen-free wearable category is having its moment in the spotlight with an explosion of new rings and wrist-based trackers from Oura, Ultrahuman, Google and Garmin promising to track long-term health trends round the clock without the battery limitations and distractions that come along with tiny smartwatch screens. But that same lack of a screen has limited how much these devices can do beyond collecting health data.

Circular, based in Paris, is carving out its own lane by pushing more functionality onto the finger. Its FDA-cleared ECG feature and AFib detection, and NFC payments and haptic alerts push the Ring 3 series closer to smartwatch territory, without giving up the low-profile design that draws people to rings in the first place.

The trade-off is that Circular’s platform still isn’t as established as competitors such as Oura, Whoop and Google, which have had more time to build out their health insights, coaching and ecosystems.

The Ring 3 lineup also expands Circular’s health tracking with blood pressure trends, glucose trend estimates and advanced sleep metrics. But without FDA clearance, these remain wellness features designed for spotting trends and more conversation starters with a doctor rather than diagnostic tools.

Circular/CNET

Circular Ring 3 Slim vs. Circular Ring 3 Pro

Both rings share Circular’s core health tracking, NFC payments and the returning haptic vibration motor, but there are some important hardware differences.

Dimensions: As the name suggests, the Ring 3 Slim is a lot smaller, in both height and width, than the Pro and the previous generation, putting it closer to the ultra-slim Oura Ring 5, which was the smallest ring I’d tested at the time. The Ring 3 Pro, by contrast, is also slightly shorter than its predecessor, but it’s gained thickness and weighs exactly the same as the Gen 2 ring.

Materials: The Pro uses titanium, while the Slim is made from a biocompatible resin with a titanium coating.

Battery: The Pro will outlast the Slim by about two days. Circular claims up to 12 days for the Ring 3 Pro, versus 10 days for the Slim.

Health tracking: Only the Pro has the ECG feature and blood pressure tracking.

Circular

Circular Ring platform and AI coach

Circular has built its following on a subscription-free model, giving ring owners full access to core health tracking metrics along with its Kira AI health companion, a feature most competitors charge for even when they offer a free tier.

However, the company isn’t fully closing the door on charging for advanced medical features, with some of these showing as “limited time” in the app. 

Price and availability

Circular hasn’t announced pricing or a firm release date for either Ring 3 model yet. The company says those details, along with preorder timing, will arrive in the coming months. We’ll update this article when the company announces more details.

title: Amazon’s Zoox expands its robotaxi service to Las Vegas airport
snippet: Zoox is expanding to this critical ride-hailing destination a few weeks after it started charging for robotaxi rides.
fullText:
Zoox isn’t wasting any time now that it’s allowed to operate and charge for rides in its custom-built robotaxi. 

The company has extended its commercial robotaxi service in Las Vegas to include rides to and from Harry Reid International Airport. Customers will be able to hail rides to the airport beginning Thursday, according to Zoox. The expansion, which unlocks a critical ride-hailing destination, builds on a series of recent wins for the Amazon-owned autonomous vehicle technology company.

Silicon Valley-based Zoox spent more than a decade developing its self-driving system and custom robotaxi that lacks traditional controls like a steering wheel and pedals. While it has made progress, even providing rides to customers in Las Vegas for a year, it wasn’t able to operate as a true commercial robotaxi service.

That changed in August after federal safety regulators gave Zoox a temporary exemption from certain motor vehicle safety standards. The commercial exemption, which lasts two years and allows Zoox to deploy up to 2,500 vehicles, spans eight federal motor vehicle standards, including windshield defrosting and light vehicle braking systems.

The exemption has kicked Zoox’s business expansion into drive. The company started charging for rides on August 10, said it would begin testing its self-driving vehicles in San Diego and Houston, and released its safety framework — all actions that point to a company ramping up operations.

Image Credits:Zoox /

The company’s expansion to the Las Vegas airport appears to give it a bit of an edge over traditional ride-hailing companies Uber and Lyft, at least when it comes to grabbing a ride from the airport into the city. According to Zoox, its robotaxi will pick up and drop off riders at both airport terminals near baggage claim. While Uber and Lyft can drop passengers off at the curb at the terminal, the pick up location is about a five- to ten-minute walk from baggage claim on the upper floor of a nearby parking garage.

Zoox is the only robotaxi company operating a service to the Las Vegas airport, but more competition is coming. 

The city has served as a testing ground for several autonomous vehicle companies over the years, and is now expected to be teeming with commercial robotaxi operators in the next year. Tesla, Uber and Waymo all received permits last month from the Nevada Transportation Authority to operate commercial robotaxi services in Clark County, home to Las Vegas. Uber plans to operate robotaxis through partnerships with Hyundai subsidiary Motional, and Zoox.

Together, these permits would allow the deployment of up to 8,000 robotaxis across the county over the next 12 months.

title: X shifts US creator payouts from Stripe to X Money
snippet: X says U.S. creator payouts will now be handled through its X Money payments service, a change that appears to replace the previous Stripe-powered payout system.
fullText:
Elon Musk’s social network X on Wednesday said that starting today, all of its U.S. creator payouts will be handled through X Money, the app’s payments service.

This includes payouts from both X’s Original Content Rewards Program and creators’ subscriptions, the company said in an update shared on X.

Starting today, U.S. payouts for Original Content Rewards and Subscriptions will be paid through @XMoney. You'll have access to your payouts the moment they’re sent.

› Already using 𝕏 Money? No action needed. Your next payout will be sent there.

› Not yet on 𝕏 Money? Open…

— Creators (@XCreators) September 2, 2026

The benefit of this new payment system is that the payments are instant. There’s no waiting until the end of a billing cycle or a minimum threshold that has to be reached before the creator can access their money. Previously, payments were processed every two weeks, with a minimum payout of $30, X’s documentation states.

However, the announcement’s wording seems to indicate that there aren’t any other options for receiving payments on the platform, meaning X is forcing creators to use X Money even if they would have preferred the prior payout method, which was powered by Stripe.

Reached for comment, a representative for X said the change is required for those in the U.S. Creators outside the U.S. will remain on Stripe. 

The shift follows other changes to X’s creator programs. On September 7, X will retire its Creator Revenue Sharing Program, which stopped accepting new members last month. Creators are being shifted instead to the Original Content Rewards Program, which, as the name implies, puts a heavier emphasis on original content.

The company’s new payments service, X Money, began supporting creator payouts earlier this month. The payments offering, a part of Musk’s broader plan to make X an “everything app,” includes a bank card with 3% cash back, instant payments, free ATM withdrawals, and other digital banking services. However, X Money is not a bank; the accounts are held at the FDIC-insured Cross River Bank.

X’s post said creator payouts will also count toward X Money users’ direct deposit requirements to receive the service’s better APY rate. Currently, the service’s website says X Premium users will get a boosted 6% rate, compared to the standard 4% rate.

In addition, X will issue a 1099-NEC for individuals receiving creator payouts. For LLCs, X will collect the organization’s W-9 information to ensure the 1099s are accurate, the company noted.

This article was updated after publication with X’s comment.

title: This video experiment perfectly illustrates my frustration with iPhone Cinematic mode
snippet: I recently observed that Apple appeared to have abandoned Cinematic mode, and a video experiment perfectly illustrates my frustration at this fact. That’s not because the feature is bad, but rather that it comes so close to being good enough for real-life use that it’s hard to see why Apple hasn’t taken advantage of the massive increases in power between the iPhone 13 on which it launched and the latest iPhones. Let me show you what I mean … more…
fullText:
I recently observed that Apple appeared to have abandoned Cinematic mode, and a video experiment perfectly illustrates my frustration at this fact.

That’s not because the feature is bad, but rather that it comes so close to being good enough for real-life use that it’s hard to see why Apple hasn’t taken advantage of the massive increases in power between the iPhone 13 on which it launched and the latest iPhones. Let me show you what I mean … 

I said previously that I understood why Apple hasn’t made updating it a priority, but also argued that it should do so to encourage future videographers and filmmakers – especially teenagers who may not have access to any other camera kit.

A friend of mine uses a smartphone to interview complete strangers passing by on the street, and somehow succeeds in having them open up in ways you could never imagine. I decided to turn the tables and put him on the stool and to likewise film using a smartphone, in this case my iPhone 16 Pro Max.

I wanted to see how well Cinematic mode could cope with a relatively simple challenge: a person in the foreground with around 25 feet of separation from railings behind him, and probably close to a thousand feet to the O2 on the opposite side of the Thames. Additionally, he would be sat on a stool, meaning rather limited movement.

The answer was … so close yet so far. The overall look is good, but there are visible halos between CK’s legs and the railings, the O2 pylons come into focus some of the time when he moves his head in front of them, and the river occasionally comes into focus when he opens his arms:

To be fair, CK argues that the average person viewing the video isn’t going to see the problem. If they are neither a filmmaker nor a techie familiar with the way the feature works, they probably won’t even notice the issues, and it won’t bother them if they do. I suspect he may well be right.

But it does bother me, and I think anyone with even amateur filmmaking ambitions will share my frustration – and that’s precisely the target market for the feature.

As I said at the outset, my frustration isn’t because the feature is bad, but rather because I genuinely believe that it could be dramatically better if Apple took full advantage of the power of the current generation of iPhone chips and the neural processing capabilities they possess. Indeed, I would expect a properly updated version of Cinematic mode to be able to cope with significantly more challenging environments than this.

Do you agree with my assessment, and would you like Apple to show cinematic mode some love? Please share your thoughts in the comments.
